subsubtopic: ALLEGED RACIST PROGRAM SHOWN ON CTV-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Whereas the Canadian Television network CTV recently produced and televised a program entitled "Campus GiveAway" on the television program "W5"; and whereas committees of Chinese Canadians objected to the program as racist; and whereas, as a result, Mr. Murray Chercover, the president of CTV, has now acknowledged that distorted statistics, combined with the visual presentation, made the program appear racist in tone and effect, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell):
That this House condemns racism in any form, applauds the efforts of the committees of the concerned Chinese Canadians, welcomes the admission of president Chercover, and urges the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission, CTV, and other media to take steps to ensure that this sort of program is never aired again.

speechtext:

Madam Speaker, before the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) leaves the House, I would like to raise a point of order with respect to his announcement this morning of what he described as the formation of six parliamentary task forces in the areas of the economy, social affairs and foreign policy. I watched on television the announcement that he made in the course of his press conference.
The Prime Minister indicated that the government House leader or someone had consulted us on the matter. 1 want to make it clear to the Prime Minister so that the record will be straight that we were not consulted in the sense that I under-
Point of Order-Mr. W. Baker
stand the word "consultation", although I was alerted by my friend yesterday as he and I were leaving the chamber that the Prime Minister would be making an announcement on a task force of some kind. There was no decision and no indication that the chairman would be appointed by the government, that the task force would appear to be responsible to a minister of the Crown rather than to Parliament. There was no indication at all as to what the membership on these task forces would be.
I thought that I should correct the record with respect to that matter of consultation. If members will read the announcements, there is a real question, and something that should be of concern to the House, as to how these task forces can be legitimately called parliamentary task forces. The only way 1 can see they can be called parliamentary in any sense of the word at all is that there is an indication that members of Parliament will be invited to serve on these task forces. I am sure that even the Prime Minister will agree that parliamentary committees, task forces, or whatever label one wishes to put on them, carry with them certain rather heavy obligations on the members.
There is a system in place to protect the members and the rights of members. For instance, fundamentally, will the minutes of the meetings of these task forces and the evidence which is given before them be recorded and will it be made public without some reference to a minister of the Crown? That is a parliamentary protection that we have, that Parliament is not subservient to the minister. To whom will these task forces be reporting? If they are reporting to Parliament, that is one thing; but what does "the responsible minister" mean, and what does it mean when it said that the Prime Minister wants advice from the task forces? Is this to be secret advice? Are members of all the parties to be co-opted to the ministry with respect to the advice?
Is there a right, for instance, for there to be a minority report from the task force, as there is right now? Are we to have the opportunity as parliamentarians to debate the efficacy of the subject matters that are set forth? Those subject matters are quite different, except in one case, from the subject matter that we had brought forward and, as well, there was a parliamentary debate in that respect. Will we have that opportunity?
Another question is, will there be a term of reference submitted for debate? There has been no discussion with respect to that matter. And what about the reports? Will they be tabled in the House? Will these task forces be reported in the usual sense so that we may have an opportunity to debate the reports? Before any matter is dealt with regarding these task forces, these are all questions which ought to be dealt with in consultation.
As I see the situation, we are departing in a great way from what is a traditional parliamentary practice with traditional parliamentary rules to safeguard and protect, not only the rights of members of Parliament, but the rights of the public in terms of the information that the public will receive from these reports.
166

April 18, 1980
Point of Order-Mr. W. Baker
Some time during the course of the question period or just prior to it there appeared on the desk of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) what purports to be a term of reference of some kind for some form of committee on disabled persons, a copy of which the hon. member delivered to me. I do not know where this document came from. No one has consulted us about the form of it, which is contrary to the usual parliamentary courtesy.
The document covers a number of areas and purports to be in the form of the normal term of reference that would be approved by the House of Commons. It says in part:
That the task force will submit reports from time to time, as appropriate, with a final report to be submitted by October 31, 1980-
It does not say to whom those reports will go, whether it be a minister of the Crown, Parliament or whatever. It purports to give this ad hoc committee the power to send for persons, papers and records. That is a power which comes out of the rules of the House of Commons. It does not come out of the air and certainly it does not come out of this piece of paper. It cannot come out of the mouth of the Prime Minister, however well intentioned it may be.
There was a House leaders' meeting on Wednesday, and we could have been consulted at that time. Rather than have the matter come up in an amicable discussion between House leaders while leaving the House, rather than suddenly having terms of references appear-for which apparently there will be no opportunity to debate-and rather than following this peremptory approach to Parliament by making the announcement of the formation of the task forces, it is advisable that some form of consultation take place.
There is also the matter of choosing the chairman. I always thought that it was the right of Parliament to choose parliamentary committee chairmen. Rather than choosing the chairman peremptorily, the Prime Minister might have been better advised if he had arranged to have the consultations in the formal manner. Perhaps he did and those consultations did not take place, I do not know. In any event, it does present Parliament, the government and certainly the opposition with a dilemma with respect to this announcement which was made this morning. It is a dilemma that will have to be resolved one way or another with regard to what is the normal parliamentary practice. Because of the importance of this matter to our institution and to the safeguards for Parliament and the public, I felt that I should raise the matter. I knew of no other way to raise it than by point of order, Madam Speaker.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-ANNOUNCEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF TASK FORCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 understand the concern of the House leader of the Conservative party and I think that he quite properly raised the matter by way of a point of order. I accept the hon. member's distinction between "informing" and "consultation".
The sequence of events is as follows. Yesterday in cabinet the government agreed to the setting up of these task forces. Therefore, there could not have been prior consultation. The government House leader quite correctly informed the other House leaders that there would be an announcement. Obviously, now that it has been announced, consultations will follow, and we will attempt to respond to all the questions raised by the hon. gentleman.
Of course, the simplest answer of all is that we were attempting to take a leaf out of the book of the Conservative party. We thought that they were quite correct in establishing not parliamentary committees as such, but task forces to inform the government. They themselves in their period of government set up three task forces to my knowledge without any consultation with my party, certainly not with myself. There were three of them, one on grain transportation, one on rail line abandonment and one on beef import legislation.
You will recall, Madam Speaker, that the question of these task forces was discussed in this House last November and December and that your eminent predecessor, Speaker Jerome, as he then was, ruled that task forces of this nature were fine, that they should be encouraged and they should be funded. I believe reference was made to one that our party had set up in 1974 when we were the government to look into the Millhaven incident. Speaker Jerome found fault with the initiative of the other side of the House only in that they were one party task forces, and if public funds were going to be spent he indicated in a gentle way that it would have been well if other members could have been part of that task force.
Our initiative, I repeat, is building on the Tory action of last summer. We are creating task forces. We think it right and proper that members of Parliament can and should be used to inform the government on particular subjects. Therefore, there is no disagreement between us. The only difference is that we have announced to the other parties that we hope some of their members would sit on these task forces.
That is where the matter rests at this stage. Consultation will follow, particularly on the terms of reference and the mode of action of that particular task force which will be discussed within the task force itself, to make sure that everyone is in agreement.
As to the members who would sit on that task force, we will await answers from the House leaders of the other parties to indicate if they are interested in joining some of our members and participating in some of these task forces. If they are, we will assemble them and seek agreement on the terms of reference. Terms of reference have been proposed but, of course, they can be modified if all parties can find some more proper way of conducting the study.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-ANNOUNCEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF TASK FORCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to just carry on for a moment with this point of order. I shall not detain the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) long in the House. We are dealing really with three kinds of instruments. There were established internally during the period of our government the series of task forces that the Prime Minister has referred to and to which the Speaker found some gentle exception. Action was taken by our governement to remedy the situation.
April 18, 1980

There was also the very clear proposal by our party when in government to establish select committees of the House of Commons to look into some of the matters which are proposed here and which were announced by the Prime Minister earlier today. Those select committees would operate with all of the force and all of the safeguards of committees of the House of Commons of Canada, which is something quite different from what I gather has been proposed by the Prime Minister.
There is also a third variant to which he made reference, and that was the assignment to a subcommittee of a standing committee of the House of Commons during one of his previous incarnations as Prime Minister of a study into the question of penitentiaries. It is not clear to us exactly what is intended here.
Clearly we on this side, assuming there could be agreement on the terms of reference, would prefer that a task force so established would have all of the power of a parliamentary select committee. We believe that provides the best protection both for individual members of Parliament and for the public. It means that a minister such as, say, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), if she received a report on the handicapped that she did not personally like, would not be in a position to hide that report. As we understand what is being proposed now, the minister has the power to hide a report that she does not like. We think that is a power which could very easily be abused and could seriously erode or undermine the parliamentary system.
It would be very helpful to us, therefore, to know exactly what is being proposed here. Our preference would be for select committees of the House of Commons. We naturally would want to have the opportunity for full discussion of the terms of reference to ensure that the ambit of inquiry was broad enough to allow members of Parliament and the interested public to have the fullest possible productive participation.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-ANNOUNCEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF TASK FORCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, may I first of all confirm what I think has now been made clear, namely, that although we were informed yesterday that this announcement was going to be made this morning, we were not consulted or asked for our consent or approval. As a matter of fact, 1 suggested that the announcement should be made in the House rather than at a press conference, but that position was not accepted. Now that the idea is out in the public arena, however, we welcome the suggestion that there will be consultation before any further action is taken.
I want to support wholeheartedly the position taken by both the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) that these tasks forces must be parliamentary committees. Maybe they will have to be set up as special committees or what have you, but certainly we as members of opposition parties do not want to find ourselves simply co-opted by ministers of the government and made servants of them for whatever their purposes may be. We think the idea of a special task force on special subjects-which after all is another way of saying a special committee study-is a good one, but we want it kept in its
Point of Order-Mr. W. Baker
parliamentary context. When there are consultations among the House leaders about these task forces, that will certainly be our position.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-ANNOUNCEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF TASK FORCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition indicated that his government had done both-had set up select committees and task forces. In the case of the Millhaven incident in 1974, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) reminds me that indeed it was a task force. I believe the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) sat on that one.
The Leader of the Opposition is confusing that task force with a subcommittee of the parliamentary committee chaired by the then member for Windsor-Walkerville, now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan). But there was a task force. We had set one up and the hon. Leader of the Opposition set some up.
He is now saying, if I understand him, that he would prefer to have select committees to task forces. Madam Speaker, his government showed that you can have both; our government shows that you can have both and we are proposing today to announce our desire to set up these task forces. We hope we will have co-operation from the other parties. If they do not want to hear of task forces in the future, although they did in the past, we will see what can be done.
Out intention is to involve members from all parties in a task force, as was done in 1974, to have all parties come together to give advice to the government of the day and, hopefully, to parliament on a specific situation, as was done in the case of Millhaven.
We are in the hands of the opposition parties. If they do not want to sit on task forces, in view of Speaker Jerome's ruling we probably would not presume to proceed with the creation of such task forces in such circumstances as were regretted by Speaker Jerome because of the unilateral manner in which it had been done by the Leader of the Opposition. We will discuss the formation of these task forces and I hope it will be possible to set them up, Madam Speaker. Members on every side of the House have frequently regretted that Parliament was being ignored, that members were not present enough at the formation of policies and that they should be involved in some way in the establishment of those policies. That is our aim.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-ANNOUNCEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF TASK FORCES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, one very brief question for clarification. Is the Prime Minister also prepared to discuss with parties on this side the establishment of select committees for the same purpose?

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-ANNOUNCEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF TASK FORCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, certainly I would hope that the House leaders of all parties would discuss, when needed, setting up such select committees.
1 think we felt when we were in the opposition that the government had perhaps overdone this a little bit in setting up that many and that Parliament could not easily manage

April 18, 1980
Point of Order-Mr. W. Baker
regular standing committees, select committees and task forces. Maybe there will be an inclination to set up less of them, but we have not at all rejected the idea of select committees as provided for under the rules of the House.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-ANNOUNCEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF TASK FORCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 would like just a brief word on this important subject because I was closely involved in the breakthrough which occurred last fall. I believe this was a breakthrough that was regarded by all members sitting in Parliament at the time as one which would allow private members of Parliament to have a direct input in developing policy at long last.
As I recall, the then opposition House leader, who is now the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen), was concerned that the proper parliamentary procedures be observed in establishing, in particular, the special select committee dealing with the subject of rehabilitation services. In fact, there was such a long delay in making sure that the parliamentary niceties would be observed that our committee did not really have final approval until November 29.
We are all aware, at least those of us who have been in the House of Commons for a number of years, that there has been a gradual erosion of the rights of private members of Parliament. The hope has always been that the committee system would remedy some of this intrusion of the executive. In most instances 1 think hon. members will agree that even the committee system unfortunately has become a creature of the government. But here in the special select committees was a breakthrough which gave for the first time parliamentarians- private members of Parliament-the right to deal with areas of urgent concern and to bring in recommendations through the regular parliamentary process.
I might add that I was the member of Parliament who had the privilege of leading off in the debate on November 29 that established finally the special select committee of Parliament. The then House leader for the opposition, now the Minister of Finance, objected to the fact that I was the lead-off speaker. I am sure hon. members will recall that debate and the then government House leader, now the opposition House leader, explained in quite explicit terms that it was a gesture that indicated that at long last private members of Parliament were going to have an important role to play in select committees. In particular, they were going to be dissociated from the influence of ministers of the Crown.
In summing up his statement at that time, the then House leader of the opposition stated this at page 1837 of Hansard for November 29:
I do not wish to embarrass any further the hon. member, who has a deep interest in this subject, but I would like to advise the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker) that it is a precedent which, I suggest, should have a very short life.
I hope that as consultations proceed on this important subject we can use the same quotation, that a task force directly responsible to a minister is a precedent which will have a very short life, and that we will return to the structure which was a real breakthrough in allowing private members to
participate independently through the select committee procedure.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-ANNOUNCEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF TASK FORCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will be very brief. I am sorry the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has left. I know he can read and I hope this will be drawn to his attention.
The Prime Minister indicated that he was approachable by other House leaders on the nature and kind of committees and whether or not there should be any. 1 have not seen the complete list. However, I was very interested during the last Parliament in the contemplated select committee on nuclear power and nuclear proliferation. There was mention of that very serious matter, not only for world peace but also for human survival, in the throne speech.
Therefore, 1 want to ask whether or not the Prime Minister or the government would be approachable on some other kinds of additions in terms of the subjects being addressed in these select committees. Perhaps that matter can be drawn to the Prime Minister's attention and an answer can be given in some other way at some other time.
[Translation\

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-ANNOUNCEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF TASK FORCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in answer to the last two members who expressed their preference for select committees I simply wan! to draw to to their attention the fact that according to Standing Order 65 there are already 20 standing committees of the House of Commons. In the past we have found it most difficult to interest more than a third of the members in actively participating in the deliberations of the standing committees of the House. 1 wonder if it is wise and advisable to plan the creation of select committees at this time before it can be demonstrated that with the already existing committees it is not possible to make the system work properly.
Still I find their suggestion interesting because it conveys to some extent the idea of a change. But, as the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) mentioned this morning, it is an original idea to which, surprisingly enough, the Progressive Conservative Party had already given some thought since they themselves had considered setting up task forces. So all we want is to allow backbenchers an opportunity to participate more directly in the decision-making process. That is a form of participation that we want and that we suggest to the official opposition party. If members opposite prefer the striking of a select committee, that could be included in new discussions on a more general parliamentary reform. I remember quite well that the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) sat as I did on a committee on procedure and organization in 1975 and 1976. We got a very interesting report on committees that had been prepared by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who is now in the House, and that contained all interesting ideas. But there were never any concrete results about that parliamentary reform so desired and so desirable, Madam Speaker.
April 18, 1980

So the action we are taking today is that intention which has been expressed by the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada to give members from all regions of Canada and particularly from western Canada a chance to participate in those committees he described this morning in replying to the right, hon. Leader of the Opposition, who is here, and to the House leader of the official opposition. That is our approach on that matter. We believe it would not be wise for the moment to add committees of the House to the twenty or so that already exist in accordance with the provisions of Standing Order 65. Now an invitation has been made to members from both sides of the House to participate. 1 am sure that the right hon. Prime Minister will not prevent backbenchers from working in a constructive way on matters of national interest. 1 am certain of it, and I am also assured of it by the House leader of the New Democratic Party.
That is all we are aiming for. We want to make members work, we want to get them more interested, we want to enhance their role. That is a first step in parliamentary reform, and I wonder why reactions are not negative. Questions asked will be the topic of negotiations between the House leaders, as required. Yesterday, I acted merely out of courtesy. I advised my colleagues that the right hon. Prime Minister was going to make an announcement. That is all I was supposed to do. We are open to any positive suggestion for improving the efficiency of the task forces. We are counting on the participation of Progressive Conservative members as well as of the NDP. As for the proposed select committees as such, I respectfully submit that this could be the topic, in the near future, of a study on parliamentary reform.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-ANNOUNCEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF TASK FORCES

Madam Speaker, 1 just want to say I am very happy to note that the government House leader has indicated that all aspects of this question will be subject to negotiations, because I think that is quite important. That is the kind of assurance my friend and I want and 1 thank him for giving us that assurance.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-ANNOUNCEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF TASK FORCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since we are given the opportunity to discuss this matter briefly, I should like to add just one more point to what the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) has said. I would co-operate with the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of his party in the House in setting up those task forces for one simple reason. I do not think we should discuss those task forces as such as select committees of the House for one reason only.
1 therefore urge them to co-operate because, whether we want to or not, a parliamentary body such as a select committee can in some cases be active and positive, especially in those cases where it is asked to play an inquisitorial role. But often political opposition in the House of Commons can make itself
Privilege-Mr. Nystrom
felt through a select committee, which is not to say that this is necessarily a bad thing. However, I do think a task force set up by order in council can be a mechanism that is more positive and efficient than a select committee of the House. But that need not mean that we will not have select committees. But I would ask the Leader of the Opposition, however, not to make co-operation on task forces conditional upon whether or not we have select committees. In some cases, I would agree with that. What I liked about his proposal last year was that in some cases task forces could make more positive studies because, despite the philosophical differences reflected in task forces, chances are they might be less imbued with party politics. As for me, 1 have agreed to be a member of a task force and 1 have invited a member of his party to become involved in it, because I feel he could study the matter very well.

subsubtopic: MR. NYSTROM-REPORTED STATEMENT BY MEMBER OF SASKATCHEWAN LEGISLATURE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I raise a question of privilege on a subject today that I find very difficult because it has racial connotations to it. That therefore makes it very difficult. It concerns a statement made by a member of the Saskatchewan legislature, Mr. Dennis Ham who, with another member who up until a few weeks ago was leader of the opposition and leader of the Conservative party in Saskatchewan, Mr. Dick Collver, left their party to sit as independents to advocate the separation of the west from Canada and the joining of the west with the United States.

Madam Speaker, I have here an article that made headlines in Le Journal de Montreal on April 17, 1980, and which I should like to quote:
If the hostages in Tehran were Quebeckers, they would say:
That is, people from western Canada.
"Leave them there".
A member from western Canada



1 will repeat that in English. If the hostages in Tehran were Quebeckers, they would say in western Canada "Leave them there".

subsubtopic: MR. NYSTROM-REPORTED STATEMENT BY MEMBER OF SASKATCHEWAN LEGISLATURE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MR. NYSTROM-REPORTED STATEMENT BY MEMBER OF SASKATCHEWAN LEGISLATURE
speechtext: Who said that?

subsubtopic: MR. NYSTROM-REPORTED STATEMENT BY MEMBER OF SASKATCHEWAN LEGISLATURE
speechtext:
A member from western Canada.

April 18, 1980
Privilege-Mr. Nystrom

But, Madam Speaker, as I said, it is not with pride that I rise on a question of privilege this morning, but an article datelined Regina from the Canadian Press says, and I quote:
If 50 French Canadians were held hostages in Tehran instead of 50 Americans, the majority of western Canadians would say, "Leave them there".
That is at least what the independent MLA for Swift Current, Mr. Dennis Ham. claimed during a conference at the Saskatchewan Press Club on Tuesday.
Mr. Ham, who has already been campaigning for some time for the secession of western Canada and its incorporation into an American state, is also predicting an uprising in Quebec.
Madam Speaker, Mr. Ham, a Saskatchewan MLA, like all other Canadians, has a right to express his opinion freely, but that opinion does not reflect at all the opinion of the people in my province of western Canada.
Unfortunately, as you know, a minority in western Canada does not understand the meaning of the aspirations of Quebeckers. But Mr. Ham's words do not reflect the opinion of that minority, let alone of the majority of the people in my province in western Canada. Mr. Ham's words were an insult to Quebeckers, to the Canadians from Saskatchewan, from western Canada and all Canadians.

Reflecting back to the speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in this House three days ago when he said that we in this House represent all of the people of Canada, as a representative of my province and my constituency I feel that a statement of this sort, made by an elected member who has as his colleague a highly respected member, distorts badly in this time in Canada the sentiments of a number of people in western Canada. Because of that, I feel it is an infringement upon my work and my ability to speak accurately for the people of western Canada, as this gentleman does not in any way whatsoever represent the feelings of people in western Canada. 1 have never found anyone who would like to have the American hostages replaced by hostages from Quebec and who would then say "Leave them there".
I want to take this opportunity to dissociate myself and the members of my party, especially those from western Canada, from the statements made by that member of the Saskatchewan legislature. I am sure the same is true of western members of the Conservative party and the Liberal party as well. If you in any way see this as a question of privilege, Madam Speaker, 1 would be prepared to move a motion that we refer this statement and articles of this sort to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for study and elaboration.

subsubtopic: MR. NYSTROM-REPORTED STATEMENT BY MEMBER OF SASKATCHEWAN LEGISLATURE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: MR. NYSTROM-REPORTED STATEMENT BY MEMBER OF SASKATCHEWAN LEGISLATURE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, briefly on the question of privilege, I doubt very much that this is a question of privilege for a House like ours. I am sure the hon. member had his own reasons to raise this issue and quote that article in the House of Commons, and I
do not want to elaborate on his motivations or his reasons. But I, as a member from western Canada, along with my colleagues, want to take this opportunity to join with the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) in the position he took, namely, that the statement attributed to Mr. Ham does not represent at all the opinion of the people in western Canada. The basic thing that should be pointed out here today is that the House of Commons is not powered to restrict the freedom of speech of members, private citizens and even of members of another House in another jurisdiction. But for us, as individuals, and myself as leader of a party with a large support in western Canada, this is an opportunity to reject outright the views that were quoted and attributed to Mr. Ham.

subsubtopic: MR. NYSTROM-REPORTED STATEMENT BY MEMBER OF SASKATCHEWAN LEGISLATURE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 must add some comments to those of my colleague from Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). As my colleague and the Leader of the Opposition said, no one would contemplate limiting the right of any individual to express his opinion. But when that individual expresses an opinion and claims or infers that his opinion is held by most people in western Canada, then that is an insult to most western Canadians.

subsubtopic: MR. NYSTROM-REPORTED STATEMENT BY MEMBER OF SASKATCHEWAN LEGISLATURE
speechtext:
It does, I believe, infringe on the privileges of members of Parliament, particularly on those from western Canada, when that kind of allegation is made so all-inclusively, asserting that some sort of general feeling, attitude or state of mind or piece of insanity is held by western Canadian people.
I want to say to you, Madam Speaker, and to my French Canadian compatriots that the French fact in all parts of Canada is what has made the major difference between our country and most, if not all, of the other countries, and particularly the difference between our country and the United States. The French fact in all parts of Canada has made us an example to the world of how peoples of different cultures can live together in peace and work together to solve differences, some of which go back decades and decades, to make our country stronger, freer, and, what is most important, more sovereign and independent.
It is not new that there have been a few people not only in western Canada but in all parts of Canada who from time to time over the last 200 years have held such views as this, but invariably those few who held such views were the kooks, flukes, flakes, freaks and right-wing reactionaries who are an infinitesimal minority of insanity. It is not just peculiar to a handful of western Canadians; it is peculiar among a handful of people in different parts of this country.
I say to my French Canadian compatriots that the opposite is the case. The great majority of western Canadians feel the opposite; they respect you and your contribution to our nation.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at the time the House adjourned last evening I was addressing my remarks to the frustrations of my constituents in Calgary South with respect to the federal government. 1 would like to say at this time that those frustrations in no way reflect the sentiment which was expressed in the newspaper article which was just described.
In my remarks I was dealing with the question of oil pricing and, in particular, I had commenced to talk about OPEC oil prices. I think that many Canadians believe that OPEC oil prices are still determined by a cartel and that these prices bear no relationship to fair market value. This was certainly the case in 1973 when the supplies of oil from OPEC countries far exceeded the demand for their oil. This has not been the case since 1978. As Sheik Yamani said several weeks ago, OPEC has lost control of price levels. In the years 1978 and 1979 the demand for OPEC oil far exceeded the supply. There is no longer a uniform OPEC price. Each OPEC country, other than Saudi Arabia, is charging whatever the market will bear.
Surely at the very least Canadians should be prepared to pay a price for domestic oil which is equivalent to the cost of developing alternative forms of energy. Failure to recognize this as a fair value for domestic oil is to put our heads in the sand in terms of achieving energy self-sufficiency.
In his speech the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated that "Prime Minister Clark was not successful in reconciling the views of the provinces of Ontario and Alberta on energy pricing". That is not the case. Our government did reach an agreement on energy pricing with all of the provinces in Canada. While neither Ontario nor Alberta were happy, the
fact of the matter is that an agreement was reached. There was a meeting of the minds and that, in my view, is a definition of an agreement.
The founding Fathers of Confederation wrote into the constitution that it was the right of the national government to uphold the national interest, even in areas of provincial jurisdiction, if such jurisdiction was being exercised in a way which was contrary to the national interest. There can be no question that the wealthier provinces of Canada must share with the less fortunate provinces, but the question is, what do we mean by share? How far does sharing go? Does it mean that one particular province should be compelled to sell its resources on a different value basis than the other provinces sell their resources? Surely this was not the intent of the Fathers of Confederation.
There is no dispute by the people of Alberta that every citizen of Canada should enjoy equality of opportunity, no matter in what part of the country he or she chooses to live. Certainly the Alberta government is not discriminating against equality of opportunity; far from it. So many people are flocking to Alberta because of the very existence of equality of opportunity.
The west must have the opportunity to develop its own economic and social objectives within the Canadian framework. That is all we want. All the west is asking for is that opportunity to develop its own social and economic objectives within the context of confederation. This is no less true for the Atlantic provinces, Quebec or any of the other provinces.
Certainly Canada needs a strong central government, but that strength must come from a feeling of togetherness that is freely given and not given under duress. In my view, national unity is not something that can be dictated by a central government. National unity must evolve from a sense of participation within confederation, and again all the west is seeking is an opportunity to participate in confederation and not be ignored or neglected.
I personally have always seen Canada as a country trying to find itself. There has not been an urgent need for the heavy hand of a central government to pull the country together and to create for us a national identity.
I believe that Canadians could knit themselves together to find a national identity for themselves. I say in all honesty that I have many misgivings about changes to our existing constitution. For all its imperfections it has given Canadians individual freedom, civil liberties and one of the highest standards of living in the world. At the same time, I am reluctantly coming to the conclusion that if we are to hold Canada together, there has to be a change in the constitution which would permit the regions of our country to achieve the diverse objectives which fulfil regional aspirations.
I do not believe that we can continue to cling to the concept that the federal government must control all economic, social, cultural, language and communication policies in Canada. Nor do I believe that Canada can or should try to become uniform with respect to these policies. More importantly, I do not

April 18, 1980

believe that the federal government can succeed in promoting national unity by enforcing a constitutional solution with respect to these policies.
Mr. Speaker, Albertans are ready and willing for constitutional change but, more importantly, they are crying out for eastern Canada to recognize them as full partners in confederation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre De Bane (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this debate on the unity of our country, I think the real question should be whether Canadians want at all costs to open their hearts and minds in order to ensure the survival of a country where Francophones and Anglophones will live together as equals and brothers or whether they prefer to turn over a new leaf in our history books and live as two sovereign and independent nations in a land called Canada.
Everything else is nothing but discussion and quibble between legal experts, constitutional lawyers or economists.
Personally, I have made up my mind and 1 want to live in a mature, fraternal, dignified and equal partnership together with all those who were the builders and the beneficiaries of this country. If by misfortune my wager based as much on my openness as on others' generosity should fall through, then, and only then, would I extol the value of a closed society.
By the way, this is the fundamental difference between my option and that of the Pequistes who have decided to close their hearts to others before trying to find out what lies in other people's hearts. You may have noticed that their rationalization is always different. For instance, a PQ supporter will tell you that he took his stand because Quebeckers pay more taxes out to Ottawa than Ottawa spends in Quebec. But if you point out to him that this is a misrepresentation and that Mr. Parizeau himself has admitted that over the last few years the federal government has spent many more billions of dollars in Quebec than that province has paid out in taxes, he still will not change his mind.
The Address-Mr. De Bane
Could it be that the present system is too inflexible and that that rigidity is the basis of his attitude? Not so. We could be reminded that Pequiste sovereignty-association was founded when Mr. Pearson was Prime Minister of Canada, a period when federalism, as Mr. Parizeau has himself recognized, has been of unprecedented flexibility. Could it be then that our system is over-centralistic? Of course not because when you remind him that out of each tax dollar paid to the federal government, the federal government retains only 32 cents and the remaining 68 cents go back to the provincial and municipal governments, he still will not be persuaded. So it is not because our system is too centralistic. May that man have endorsed the PQ philosophy because federal policies relating to Quebec are ill-conceived and ineffective? Not so. Once again this is only a pretext because 1 have never seen a Pequiste who would be willing to abandon his option whether or not, for the sake of discussion of the federal government was willing to go along with any policies he wishes. In fact, this question was asked recently to the Quebec minister responsible for economic development, Mr. Bernard Landry, who was saying that federal policies were not to the advantage of Quebec. Reporters asked him: In the eventuality that these policies were amended as you wish, would you become a federalist? He admitted that of course he would not and that he would remain a supporter of independence.
Mr. Speaker, this shows that all the arguments used to try to explain the independence option are only a smokescreen. Basically, there are not two reasons for wanting independence, there are not three, there is only one: It is because a certain group speaks French and the others English. All the other arguments used to try to justify this option are only a smokescreen. As a matter of fact, the Parti Quebecois is now admitting that what it wants basically is to break up a relationship which exists in this country where Francophones and Anglophones together govern the largest country in the world after the Soviet Union. I therefore wonder why they want to hide the basic reason for their option and give out so . many reasons which have nothing at all to do with the 1 philosophy of their party.
In this regard, Mr. Speaker, I would like to recall the low blow dealt by Mr. Claude Morin, minister of intergovernmental affairs in Quebec, who stated recently that the only people who could suffer from the consequences of their option are those who represent Quebec in this House. In my 12 years as member of Parliament and now as minister, I never thought that a fellow Quebecker would dare make such an insidious attack against people who do not agree with him politically. Indeed, who are those people who are now preaching independence? Who are they whose administration has been stamped with incompetence? We must recall that for years they criticized their predecessors for having undertaken the James Bay project and that as soon as they were elected, they admitted

April 18, 1980
The Address-Mr. De Bane
what was very obvious, that this might have been the wisest decision made by the former government.
For years, they have argued that nuclear power should be developed without delay, before hydropower. Look what happened immediately after they came to office. Mr. Bernard Landry, who reminded us that there has always been a 2 per cent difference between the unemployment rate in Ontario and in Quebec, must admit today that, for the first time in history, the gap between the two provinces has systematically exceeded 3 per cent during the first three years of their administration, whereas it had always stood at 2 per cent or less during the years previous to 1976, 1977. It was 2.5 per cent in 1976, 3.3 per cent in 1977, 3.7 per cent in 1978 and still over 3 per cent in 1979. This had never been the case before they came to power.
Look at their budget. Out of $17 billion, they will be spending over $10 billion on social and education programs alone. The hon. minister Lazure himself indicated that for every patient treated in Quebec costs amount to over 30 per cent of the costs in Ontario.
In the area of education, I should like to quote a few excerpts from Mr. Parizeau's budget speech. Having recognized on page 34 that-
Quebeckers are overtaxed.
-he added on page 15 that he agreed, during the latest round of collective bargaining, to admit 1,600 more teachers within the system. He said:
In my opinion, this is the settlement's only inconsistent and stupid aspect.
He added:
Had we known at the time these offers were made what we know now about the actual cost of education, such offers would never have been made.
Here is what the minister of finance stated three and a half years after taking over the financial administration:
If I had known what I know today, I would have done that a month ago.
And on page 24, Mr. Parizeau stated-
We have even come to a point where our annual costs per student in our schools are $500 higher than in Ontario. That is nothing to be proud of.
In those two departments alone which engulf more than 50 per cent of his budget, we see what the minister himself and the minister of health are admitting. Fortunately, the department of highways does not come under federal jurisdiction because they would say, of course, that, if the highways in Quebec have become the biggest death traps in the province, the federal government is to be blamed.
But given their incompetence, Mr. Speaker, I have tried to demonstrate on the basis of their own statements-and history will bear witness to it-that the greatest harm they have done to our country has been the division that they created and fostered between Quebeckers of all origins. We shall never be overly stressing the extent of the damage they did during the
last 15 years by having our people and particularly our youth believe that federalists are not as patriotic as they are, that they do not love Quebec as much as they do, that they are themselves more patriotic, that they monopolize patriotism. And even on the day Mr. Trudeau was elected with the support of the population to govern Canada, one should remember all that they did to destroy him, and by the same token to undermine everything that we did. They have the gall to chastise us for not progressing fast enough. The most important legislation passed by all sides of this House, with the support of each and every member, from all parties, has been, of course, the Official Languages Act which, in section 2, sets French and English on an equal footing. Remember what Rene Levesque and the others had to say on that occasion.
Because they deny us the opportunity of doing our job in our country, they are trying today to win us over to their cause, drawing us within a society which, in spite of all their artifices will be nothing but a closed society. While they pretend to be of a social democratic strain, to foster division they went as far as supporting the Socreds from the very beginning until the last election. I think they are trying to hide under that ambiguity the fact that they want to enhance their national values at all costs. And of course, this ambiguity is also flagrant in the question they will be asking the people of Quebec. In the first part they say, and I quote, that they want the exclusive power to make legislation, to levy taxes, to establish external relations. This for sure amounts to independence. In the same question they want a mandate to conduct negotiations between a sovereign Quebec and Canada. But if the question specifies that both mandates are to be fulfilled as one, "at the same time", as the wording puts it, it remains true that the two are quite different in themselves. And that should be obvious to anybody.
Independence, sovereignty, separation, secession, all that can be decided among Quebeckers alone but if one can decide on his own whether he is going to divorce or get a separation, it takes two to decide upon marriage or association. Therefore nothing would be possible if on referendum day the answer is Yes to the question asked by the Levesque government, because Canada would not have been consulted about any association with a sovereign Quebec. And Mr. Levesque has given the rest of Canada, which incidentally has no reason to say Yes, all the reasons in the world to say No since he himself has stated many times that sovereignty and association cannot be dissociated.
On this planet where there are 2,500 languages and cultures but merely 160 countries, there have been many other movements toward separation and independence, but I know none which was marked from the start by ambiguousness and humiliation. To say that something that cannot be negotiated, like independence, will now be indissolubly linked to association, is a most humiliating statement, because it means that we
April 18, 1980

who are supposed to be the embodiment of pride are putting our future into the hands of someone else. I say, Mr. Speaker, that as far as bargaining power is concerned, I have seen better and that when you want to bluff, you do not start by showing your cards to your opponent.
Is it possible, anyway, to imagine that Canada would say yes? In my opinion, there is but one possibility left for such a scheme. It is the hypothesis of a ruined sovereignty, of a sovereignty on paper only, a sovereignty where we would share the same currency while being a minority as far as monetary decisions are concerned. I recall what Mr. Parizeau himself said three or four years ago: If Quebec has the same currency as a country whose economy would be stronger than its own, it would become a banana republic. This is what is offered to us; to remain in the wake of another country which would have a permanent right of veto in all economic areas.
How can anyone have the nerve to say that it is a challenging outlook on the future? Let us wonder for one moment how long an individual from Trois-Rivieres, Matane, Bois-Francs or Beauce would be willing to leave his or her fate in the hands of a man from Vancouver, Toronto or elsewhere? For how long? Is there another country in the world which gives a right of veto on its daily fate to another country? In my opinion it is the only hypothesis which would be accepted by the other country. Besides, it is not for nothing that Canada, which has very close relations with the United States, has never asked for an association because we know quite well that to the extent that we could have a right of veto on their policies they would have one on us and we would then remain in their wake. This is why I never heard of any sensible person in Canada who would dare approve such a solution.
Let us consider for a minute how much that thesis is unrealistic. Let us consider the opposite hypothesis. If the western provinces, which are now substantially richer than the rest of Canada and have a larger population than Quebec, decided tomorrow to separate, after their separation from Canada they could say to Quebec, Ontario and the maritimes: The western provinces will have one vote and Quebec 30 per cent of a vote.
And Ontario, which is even more densely populated than we are, will have 40 per cent of one vote, and the maritimes the balance. Would it be accepted? Is it possible to disregard realities and to think that through legislation Quebec, which has almost three million fewer inhabitants than Ontario, will turn tomorrow to Ontario and say, "we in Quebec, we have one vote and you Ontario, even with your greater population, you as well as the west and the maritimes will have one vote, and if you do not agree, I shall remain in Canada." What kind of ruse is this, if not an attempt to humiliate Quebeckers collectively to lead them to a dead end where we shall all be humiliated, an attempt, by insulting our people, to urge them to take a step, whereas, according to every survey, the percentage of independentists is strictly the same after twenty years?
The Address-Mr. De Bane
Mr. Speaker, on that proposition which, I think, is totally unrealistic, which is a dead end which would humiliate all of us who form the government of this country, who have just been mandated with far more support than the PQ, we ask the population to really show some self-respect and urge them to make with us a mature decision for the future, an enlightened choice that has nothing to do with wishful thinking, a courageous choice that will not confuse obliviousness and audacity, a logical choice that will not be dictated either by the economic or the cultural components. In sum, a choice rather than the failure to choose as proposed by the promoters of sovereignty-association.
It is quite ironical that if tomorrow Quebec accepted sovereignty-association, a number of policies it can now establish in total liberty would no longer be possible tomorrow. Whether it be the selective repeal of the sales tax in the fiscal field, industrial development incentives or preferential buying policies, all this can be done today but will no longer be possible tomorrow without the agreement of the other country next door, assuming that country agreed to enter into a common market.
Mr. Speaker, what is most saddening to me is that a large number of my fellow Quebeckers who are totally opposed to the independence concept feel compelled to vote Yes, if only to express our pride. I am not tempted like Camille Laurin to suggest, that I am the embodiment of Quebec's soul, quite the opposite, I feel that those who are ready to lead us all together into humiliation in order to make their point have in the back of their minds something much different than a language of pride and dignity. One thing I can tell them, they have no monopoly on the passion for Quebec. That passion we have as much as they do, and to me no scheme is more diabolical than the drawing of cheques on Quebeckers' patriotism, on that goal we all share of living in dignity.
This, Mr. Speaker reminds me of one of the most severe crises we went through, the conscription during the Second World War. One of its heroes was Andre Laurendeau. During that period where the whole world saw it as a duty to share in the defence of freedom, we believed in Quebec, everyone without exception, that we could not be on the side of liberty, participation in the war. Laurendeau who fought so hard against conscription wrote in his book, and I quote:
That crisis went deep. It moved us. It changed some of our ideas. Then it seemed to be over . . . out of common agreement we stopped referring to it, as if on either side we were not that proud of what we had done.
Of course, had I lived during that period and had I been told that it was patriotic to refuse to be used as cannon fodder for England, that it was once again a matter of fighting to defend the Empire, I would have said no. But now these passions have waned and we realize that in fact the Second World War was fought to defend freedom. Today they are trying to rekindle

April 18, 1980
The Address-Mr. Hargrave
our fellow citizens' patriotism by telling them that a Yes vote is a vote for dignity.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, I think I have shown they are trying to impair irretrievably the dignity and pride of the people in Quebec. For our part, we offer them something infinitely more encompassing. Rather than have a country based on religion, as emphasized by the Tremblay royal commission hardly 25 years ago, they want one founded on race or language; we invite our fellow countrymen from Quebec along with other Canadians of all regions to make up an open, brotherly society based on mutual aid. We want them to be part of Canada, but not because Canada spends more money in Quebec-if that were the reason we would not deserve to be Canadians.

speechtext:
Furthermore, the word "federal" comes from the Latin word foedus, or a pact, with fides which means confidence, promise, commitment, obligation, wish. The idea of a pact does not conjure up only a solemn promise between two or more people to have confidence in one another and to respect a commitment. It also suggests co-operation, reciprocity, mutual aid. It is not just by whim that the great French political scientist Raymond Aron stated recently that federalism is wisdom and fraternity applied to politics. A great minister in the de Gaulle administration, who is still a minister in France, Alain Peyrefitte, said recently in his book: "Le mal frangais
Many people think that France has a great advantage, owing to its unitary system. However, after observing the scene for three decades, I am convinced that polycentric countries-
And he mentions the Swiss, German and United States federations-
-that the polycentric countries constitute more flexible societies.
These are the words of the minister of justice in France, Alain Peyrefitte, who has studied the unitary and polycentric systems for three decades.
Mr. Speaker, where we want to lead Quebeckers is toward an open, fraternal society, that will participate within a country in this system of mutual aid, fraternity, co-operation. Ask a Frenchman, a German, an Englishman, a Spaniard, an Italian, what is their impression of us and they will tell you that we are by far the luckiest people in the world. That is my most deep-seated conviction.
Recently, in a world survey, Gallup found out that the happiest people live in Canada. People in France were asked in a recent survey in what country other than their own they would most like to live. The country that came far ahead of all others was Canada.
A Canada that for us is a land of freedom, a Canada where the relationships between French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians will be characterized by equality and fraternity,
a Canada that will be even more generous toward its people who suffer, are sick or poor, and precisely because we will be still richer in the years to come, a Canada that will be interdependent with all other countries of the world. A Canada that, for all of us, for each and every one of us, will keep on being a challenge to our intelligence and an appeal to open our hearts.
And I conclude with this thought of Saint-Exupery, Mr. Speaker, that the noblest profession of man is to unite men.

speechtext:
I want to begin today, Mr. Speaker, by saying it is a personal privilege for me to participate in this throne speech debate. I should like, first of all, to extend my congratulations and best wishes to Madam Speaker on her very significant appointment. I should also like to commend the mover and seconder of the address in reply for their well prepared and ably delivered lead-off speeches.
In my remarks today I intend to discuss several serious issues of special concern to our western prairie provinces, issues that I would describe as much too important to be dealt with in a partisan political manner.
I want to begin by talking about energy, drought, and a lost generation. Alberta's present-day energy resources are really the end result of a fortunate accident in climate and geography that involved dinosaurs and tropical growth many, many millions of years ago.
During the late 1920s and the 1930s I well remember the numerous gas wells, all appropriately called oil wells because that was what their drillers were looking for, on widespread range lands adjacent to our ranch operation in south east Alberta where I still live today. These gas wells had located gas without any trouble, were able to produce, and in some cases were blowing off uncontrolled into the atmosphere. There were no pipelines, of course, and no markets for this early natural gas.
It was not until about 1940 that the Alberta government introduced and passed the necessary Alberta legislation to export both oil and natural gas to other provinces and to the United States of America.
It was also another accident in climate and geography that brought on the great North American drought throughout all of the 1930s, and covering our three prairie provinces in Canada. Coinciding exactly with this continental disaster, was the ten years of business depression. That ten years of drought and depression was, in reality, half a generation lost, followed immediately by another half generation in a sort of recovery phase. We had to learn again how to handle money, how to
April 18, 1980

borrow and spend it, and that may sound strange today. That was the period of our history when small "c" conservatism was truly entrenched in the west, and especially in Alberta.
While our economies began to turn around in the mid 1940s, it was really only during the 1960s that our western prairie economies truly began to come back. We are only now regaining that lost generation of 40 years ago. This is the reason we now value so highly those energy resources that lie below the soils that drifted so disastrously in the 1930s. I ask hon. members most sincerely to try to understand that Alberta's present Heritage Fund of about $6 billion does not even begin to make up for that lost drifted soil and that lost generation 40 years ago.
I remind the House of this grim history of our western prairies because of my deep concern that the same combination of climate and geography could bring about another drought, even ten consecutive years of it. In spite of immense improvements in agricultural technology, there is no reason why another drought could not occur again all across North America, in the interior, of course.
For our cultivated crops, the results would be exceedingly serious, but not as severe as in the 1930s, thanks to our incredibly sophisticated mechanical farm equipment, and more so, thanks to our chemical herbicides-provided we will be allowed to use them.
During the 1930s, one weed, Russian thistle, single-handedly destroyed thousands of acres of spring seeding, because once the seed was in the ground and sprouted there was no way of controlling Russian thistle other than by plowing down the crop, and, of course, there was insufficient moisture to reseed if that was the course that was followed.
For our western grass pastures it is a different story. The consequences of another drought will be just as serious as that first one for those of us involved in grass growing. There are 45 million acres of grasslands presently used for domestic livestock production in western Canada. Grass, hay, surface stock-water and local flood schemes would suffer severely.
Some members may recall the remarks pertaining to a one-year western drought in 1977 that I made on various occasions in this House. Our mountain snow pack that year was only about 60 per cent of the average. That was the lowest snow pack since 1941 and our 950,000 acres of intensive irrigation just barely survived the growth season that year. Not generally known is that the cities of Calgary and Regina had dangerously low domestic water supply levels. Calgary was within three days of initiating water rationing. A sustained drought now would have a far more serious impact on our entire western prairie human population because of the enormous increase in the demand for water.
The three southern cities of Calgary, Lethbridge and Medicine Hat in Alberta and the three cities of Moose Jaw, Regina and Saskatoon in Saskatchewan have seen their total populations increase from 230,680 in the mid-1930s to well over one million today. That is a 337 per cent increase over 45 years.
The Address-Mr. Hargrave
Add to this the substantially increased water demand from the many hundreds of smaller towns and thousands of individual farms and rural acreages, all with automatic dishwashers, laundries and flush toilets. Of course, very few of the latter group I have just mentioned enjoyed this running water luxury in the 1930s.
I suggest that we all read again the startling evidence presented to the Standing Committee on Regional Development in November, 1979, when PFRA officials, Dr. Harry Hill and Mr. Collinson, were witnesses. Mr. Collinson pointed out that the cost of producing electricity throughout the prairies was an extra $100 million in 1977 because the snow pack in the Rockies was so short. I want to commend Dr. Harry Hill for his initial consideration of this matter relating to drought since he assumed his responsibilities not long ago with the PFRA.
In addition, I would like to remind all concerned of the personal suggestion that I was privileged to make before that same committee calling for a small select parliamentary committee review of PFRA, including its past history, its present status and its future role as the appropriate federal agency to assemble and implement a suitable drought contingency program. This suggestion received all-party support in November, 1979.
It should also be noted that the Canada West Foundation, located out of Calgary, has recently initiated a western Canada water resources project to provide an information base and define the problems, the most important of which in my opinion is drought.
I can assure the House that I am not desirous of deserving the doubtful distinction of being the drought conscience of this Parliament, but we should be doing much more than reminiscing about these matters in 1980. Our southern prairies have just emerged from a very mild winter with very little snow. In reality it was a winter drought, and there is presently very little soil moisture to sustain whatever spring growth is now occurring.
On a related matter, the federal government has a longstanding commitment to repair the Bassano dam on the Bow River in southern Alberta. Certain complex legalities concerning the ownership of this streambed have delayed this long overdue repair. I say we should get on with this undertaking, and if the legal complications cannot be resolved, then the Eyremore site somewhat downstream should be proceeded with.
There is one final suggestion 1 would like to make concerning drought. We should be proceeding now with long-range water planning. This includes serious consideration of northern Alberta river diversions to southern Canada. This sort of thing takes years of planning and involves both federal and provincial governments. In the west it will be the three prairie governments who will be involved and it must be undertaken within the provisions of the prairie provinces water apportionment agreement.

April 18, 1980
The Address-Mr. Hargrave
I want to turn now to another very emotional issue not related to anything 1 have said up to this point but nevertheless a very important issue. We are all very much aware of the Quebec referendum and the national public debate it has generated. Of course, this debate has made us conscious of that. However, 1 want to bring to your attention an issue that deals with the Crowsnest Pass freight rates. Debate on this issue is presently under way in western Canada and in its own significant way it is almost as important to the west, and even to Canada, as the issue I have just mentioned.
During the last two years there have been some excellent public debates at various annual agricultural meetings and symposiums throughout the western provinces. The subject is now freely discussed with much less emotion than it was for many years when it was rarely, if ever, raised in a formal way. But this debate is only taking place in western Canada. There has never been a proper formal parliamentary debate on this Crowsnest Pass freight rate issue.
The closest approach to such a debate was a Conservative opposition day which took place on May 26, 1977, when we discussed the Hall report. It seems that we all avoid a direct debate on this issue by a variety of points of view on the deliberately vague phrase "the Crow benefits". Various contributing issues dealing with such things as hopper cars, producer cars, switching, off-board quotas and our domestic feed grain policy, are really symptoms of the basic problem, namely the Crow freight rate.
Thanks to Carl Snavely's report, we now know what it costs to move our prairie grain, and that knowledge is now generally accepted by all concerned. Surely this political reality is now apparent; that our two railways cannot be ordered or forced to haul grain at less than compensatory rates.
With a majority Parliament that may very well last for as long as four years or more, this Thirty-second Parliament should have a formal Crowsnest Pass freight rate debate complete with a standing committee whose members would travel throughout the prairie provinces, possibly in about two years. That will give us another two years for the informal debate to develop. In the interval, before such a debate, would it not be appropriate to request the Supreme Court of Canada to examine and rule not on the legality of those statutory Crow rates-that point is surely not in question-but on the often repeated claim that the profits of various CPR subsidiaries be used by that railway, namely the CPR, to supplement their inadequate freight revenues on grain. Some of those subsidiaries are Cominco, Pine Point Mines, Marathon Realty and literally dozens of others that are closely related to the CPR.
It seems to me that this carefully considered and serious suggestion is a necessary preliminary step to a meaningful parliamentary debate on the Crow freight rate issue, and I hope it receives serious consideration.
I want to turn now to another issue that I think is disturbing many of us throughout the country. I think it has been referred to once or twice in this throne speech, but I want to put forward one or two ideas of my own. I refer to the metric issue.
1 sincerely hope that all members do not underestimate how disturbing and controversial the metric issue is. It has been a serious and disturbing issue throughout two election campaigns and continues to be.
Here is my considered opinion on how we might deal with metrication. We should allow the present status of metrication to remain unchanged, that is, no changeover deadlines such as those scheduled for January 1, 1981, but allow for voluntary participation in those sectors which wish it, unless one of two courses is adopted. First, there should be a proper, formal debate on metrication in all stages proceeded with in this Parliament, including a travelling standing committee stage across Canada. Incidentally, if we have such a debate, it will be the first formal debate on metrication to take place in the Parliament of Canada. Over the past 11 years there has been an off and on informal debate only.
The second possibility, and this is my preference, is that we proceed with a formal agreement or treaty with the United States which provides for both countries to proceed together on the metric changeover. Until we can agree on a date and schedule for acting together, we should not proceed.
Before I conclude, I want to make a brief but very specific mention of something in the throne speech that really pleased me. Up until now I have not said a word about my special labour of love, the cattle industry. That may surprise some members. However, there were three or four words in the throne speech that pleased me very much. There was mention of a meat import law. I would be much less than human if I did not say how pleased I was to see that. I am very anxious to get some details from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) especially with regard to how he proposes to define the term "meat" rather than "beef", which is my favourite. It no doubt has some connotations which are a little different, but the fact that this reference is in the throne speech is worthy of comment and I appreciate its being there.
In conclusion, I wanted to cover subjects in my remarks that are too important for partisan politics. I hope my hon. friends in this House will agree that these are in that category; they are at least in my opinion.
