speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to congratulate you on your election as Speaker of this House. You are the first woman ever to hold this important office, and I am convinced that you feel much pride in your appointment. I am also proud of the fact that it is to a Quebecker that this historic honour has been conferred. I hope that in the next and subsequent centuries, a great number of women, including a great number of Canadian women and people from Quebec, will follow in your footsteps.
As you know, Madam Speaker, my hopes concerning the role in the House of Quebec men and women may not be realized. Last Tuesday, Mr. Levesque announced that the referendum would be held on May 20. The PQ is seeking the mandate to end all participation in the Canadian Parliament of the duly elected representatives of the people of Quebec. It is seeking a mandate to make you the last woman from Quebec to hold the office of Speaker of the House. It is seeking a mandate to make Pierre Elliott Trudeau the last Quebecker to hold the office of Prime Minister of this country, and the mandate to make me the last Quebecker to be justice minister of Canada, and so on for all the other Quebeckers who are in the House today.
For the past 113 years this House has been at the centre of Canadian history. If it is exceptional, it is because it is the only forum where the elected representatives from all regions of Canada can meet. We all try to formulate to the best of our ability the aspirations, ideas and interests of our constituents. We listen to what other members have to say and try to understand fully the wealth and diversity of our country.
The PQ is asking for a mandate which would forever leave vacant the 75 Quebec seats in the House, a mandate which would prevent 75 men and women elected by the people from being present to express the will of Quebeckers to live a better life within a better Canada. During the next few weeks, we shall fight to make sure that Quebeckers continue to occupy in the Canadian Parliament the seats to which they are entitled. Madam Speaker, I do not think that the people of Quebec want to break up Canada. I urge them to avoid the trap which the PQ has prepared for them in the referendum. That party used to display some measure of honesty. It said openly that its objective was independence, separation. Even now, at times it does express its intentions clearly as it did, for instance, on March 16, 1977, when Mr. Levesque stated in the National Assembly that, and I quote:
The Address-Mr. Chretien
Our political option is to break away from the federal system. That is our objective: independence, sovereignty. There is no point in mincing our words.
That statement is a slip of the tongue, an accidental admission, because the aim of the whole PQ strategy is to hide the real intentions of the party behind a flow of reassuring words, such as sovereignty-association, true confederation, sovereignty with association and a new agreement. The truth of the matter is that the new agreement he means in 1980 is nothing other than the separation he spoke of in 1968. Under the disguise of all those words, Mr. Levesque and the PQ are every bit as separatist as ever. It would be a tragedy for a majority of Quebeckers to give a mandate to the PQ. They would then have rallied to a cause whose premises they do not believe in. They would then make a renewed Canada far more remote, when in fact that is the Canada they really want. The government of Canada knows full well that the people of Quebec are acutely aware of the need for change. Unfortunately, the PQ created a climate in Quebec in which it is difficult to judge the importance of what changes have already been made, and the value of what we already have in Canada. Doubtless, Canada has achieved a lot. Federalism has evolved considerably.
Let us look at a few examples. The institutions of the government of Canada were changed forever by the Official Languages Act, as my colleague the hon. member for Matane and Minister of Regional Economic Development (Mr. De Bane) put it so eloquently a few minutes ago. We now have a highly developed system of federal-provincial consultation which has transformed the relationships between the federal and provincial governments. You can see it at all first ministers' meetings which have become an annual event.
Since the war which perforce was an era of centralization, fiscal and financial agreements within the Canadian federation have changed radically. In 1945, provincial and municipal governments controlled only 31 per cent of all government revenues, after transfers. In 1960, their share was nearly 50 per cent, and in 1979 they controlled no less than 67 per cent of public revenues in Canada. In view of those figures, it can be said, as the Parti Quebecois does, that Canada is a highly centralized or a centralizing country. Behind those significant figures are other changes of very great importance. Take, for example, the parallel creation in 1965 of the Canada and the Quebec pension plans which gave the government of Quebec enormous sources of investment. For example, the 1974 agreement on family allowances allowed a major federal program to be geared to the particular needs of each of the provinces. And 1 do not have to stress the importance of the established programs financing agreement in 1976.
Canadian federalism has changed spectacularly in another financial area, namely equalization payments to the least privileged provinces. Equalization payments amounted to only $46 million in 1957-58. They have soared to $3.3 billion today and represent one of the central elements of modern federalism

April 18, 1980
The Address-Mr. Chretien
in Canada. That benefit of Canadian federalism will provide Quebec this year with an amount of $1.6 billion, more than 50 per cent of the whole program. That is the equivalent of $262 or more than $1,000 per family of four. None of those changes-and I mentioned only a few of the more important examples-suggest that our federalism is fixed or unchanging. Those major changes were possible without having to amend formally the written constitution of our federation. These changes prove that it is possible to renew the Canadian federation. As you are aware, the writing of a new constitution remains a fundamental objective for all Canadians. Since there is no amendment formula, we must do our utmost to reach a consensus among the partners in the federation about a new constitution. I suggest such a consensus is emerging at this time. It can be seen in the various proposals made by most provincial governments, by all parties in this House, by the Pepin-Robarts Commission, by the Canadian Bar Association, and many others. Although different in many respects, these proposals all agree on the core of the reform. They all call for a modernization of the distribution of powers, for bettering the central institutions, for constitutional safeguards concerning fundamental civil rights for Canadians and linguistic rights for minorities throughout the country, and also for a renewal of the role of the federal government in distributing the wealth of the country in order to ensure equal opportunities for all Canadians.
But what did the Parti Quebecois do regarding this growing consensus? It adamantly rejected any federal solution to the problem of Canada. It is absolutely not interested in the renewal of Canada. What it wants is a mandate to negotiate the end of Canada and the creation of an independent and separate state. It is not seeking a mandate to come and sit at the conference table to negotiate. It only wants to come and demand independence and association. It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that to give such a mandate to a political party that has always rejected any federal solution can in no way help the renewal of Canadian federalism.
Thus the argument that the Parti Quebecois, if given a mandate, will be able to start negotiations and reach a compromise does not hold. Such a mandate would have exactly the opposite result in that it would generate much uncertainty and foster a significant deterioration of the relations within Canada. It would certainly jeopardize the will to change which has has been evident and it would postpone for several years the constitutional reform.
What is more serious is the fact that it could cause positions to harden and create misunderstandings which could result in a division of our country.
It is appropriate to mention that in its campaign, the PQ has emphasized the absurd idea that a mandate given to a separatist party would bring about a constructive change and promote a new deal. I repeat that the new deal of 1980 is in fact the separation of 1968. Only the words have changed!
I trust in the common sense of my fellow Quebeckers. They will look into the details of the PQ's proposal before making up their mind. They will find that the mandate the Parti Quebecois requests is aimed at putting an end to the Parliament of Canada, the Canadian nationhood, the role now played by Canada on the international scene and to the benefits derived by all Quebeckers from our resources.
All Canadians are justifiably proud of the significant position held by our country on the world scene. Canada has greatly contributed to the allies victory during World War II. She played a decisive role in the creation of the United Nations and other major international organizations set up after the war, like NATO. Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Pearson, through their statesmanship, have made Canada's name well known during the forties, the fifties and the sixties. Today, Canada is governed by a man who is recognized as one of the great leaders of the western world. The Parti Quebecois is asking for a mandate to put an end to all that.
It would be the end of a Canada endowed with the greatness, confidence and historic ties which gave her a unique role in the world. Quebeckers would no longer have the right to carry the Canadian passport which is so respected. The Parti Quebecois is asking for a mandate to divide and to reduce the presence of Canada in the world, a mandate to create two small countries next to a giant, two bitter countries which will distrust each other and which will be isolated in an unstable and uncertain world.
If you doubt for a minute that the Parti Quebecois is committed to independence just read last week's newspapers in which Mr. Rene Levesque recognizes that a PQ victory in the referendum would be a mandate to create a separate army in Quebec. This is what a new deal means: a separate army, a separate country. PQ members are also asking for a mandate to negotiate an end to the wealth sharing process in Canada. The so-called association they propose would only be a vague reflection of the true economic association which exists at present. In their so-called economic association, Quebeckers would lose what they now have, namely their share in the Beaufort Sea, the Athabasca tar sands, the prairies' wheat, the offshore resources of the Pacific coast and Atlantic oil resources, etc. Canada's strength lies in the fact that all Canadians are partners sharing common resources. The separatists are asking for a mandate to deprive Quebeckers of these riches. The PQ proposition is all the more stunning that it means the relinquishment of other riches that are vital to Quebec. For example, Quebec asks for a mandate to negotiate an end to the sharing of revenue derived from Canadian taxes and Canadian oil supply to Quebec. In both cases, Quebec stands to lose a great deal. Actually what does a mandate to negotiate the end of the sharing of tax benefits mean?
April 18, 1980

Mr. Speaker, it amounts to a mandate to increase Quebec provincial income tax by 33 per cent should it wish to retain the same social services; a pension, family allowances, contribution to various provincial expenses, and so forth. In any case, they would have to find $900 for each household, or a total of $1.4 billion. That will be another hole that Mr. Parizeau will have to fill, the independence hole. Let's not forget that Quebeckers are already paying the highest taxes in Canada. For example, they pay 21 per cent more than their western neighbours, the Ontarians, and 28 per cent more than the average resident of the other nine provinces. The PQ also puts a great deal of emphasis on the need for Quebec to have full control over its resources.
As a Quebecker, I am proud of the success of Hydro-Quebec. However, 1 am not blind to some fundamental facts which are as follows: Quebec is relatively poor as far as energy is concerned. In 1978, it produced only 38 per cent of the energy it used. While it has exported some electricity, it imports all of its natural gas, oil and coal. Hence Quebec is very lucky to be a part of Canada, which produces more energy than it uses. Quebec has benefitted directly from Canadian energy resources in two ways: first, by paying for western Canadian oil at a price much below the international price; second, by receiving a substantial grant which enables it to buy foreign oil at the Canadian price.
These two advantages mean for Quebec a saving of $3.8 billion. The PQ makes no mention of this in its so-called economic association. In effect, it is asking for a mandate to negotiate an end to the grants. This will add a further $1,250 to the energy bill of the average Quebec family of four. That is the kind of mandate the PQ is seeking in the field of energy.
Mr. Speaker, I may have quoted too many figures, and I apologize, but I think it is important for my colleagues and myself to take this opportunity to correct certain misconceptions. I am privileged, Mr. Speaker, to have sat in this House for 17 years and served my country as a Minister of the Crown for over 12 years. I came to Ottawa in 1963 with some of my colleagues, with some apprehensions of the federal system. But I have learned much about Canada. I have had the privilege for six years, one month, three days and two hours to be Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and that is how I learned what Canada was all about. I have learned for example that in Arctic settlements there are more sedimentary rocks than in Louisiana, Oklahoma, Texas and California, but I will not dwell on those economic aspects.
I had the privilege to look after citizens of this country who were here before the French-speaking and English-speaking people came-the Indians and the Eskimos. And in the mandate I was given,I had to speak to them about their belonging to Canada. And you do not know how proud I was to be able to tell them that in Canada they could be what they were, Indians and Inuits, and at the same time full-fledged Canadi-
The Address-Mr. Chretien
ans. It is possible in this country to keep our linguistic and cultural differences, it is possible for those people who were the first citizens on this soil to share a historical cultural heritage unlike ours, and at the same time share the benefits and the responsibilities of Canadian citizenship.
We have made enormous progress in our society. What irks me a little in the on-going emotional debate in Quebec is that they are still talking about the mistakes of the past, a time when there was a lot of discrimination before Canada grew into a more mature society. Of course there was discrimination. But there is no point, Mr. Speaker, in trying to rewrite history. I too would have liked Montcalm to be able to defeat Wolfe on the Plains of Abraham. I was not there to wake up Montcalm when Wolfe arrived in the night. There is no point in wanting to rewrite history.
But take today's reality. The other day I was in Toronto and 1 was really moved by something I saw. A man of Italian origin who had arrived in Canada with a bag on his back when he was very young and single went up to the mike. He has now become a very successful businessman. I was at a meeting where there were 500 or 600 people, generally of ethnic groups, to honour a person of Jewish faith. That man of Italian origin said: When 1 was a little boy 1 went to a swimming pool where you had to pay 5 cents. I had my 5 cents. When I got to the door I was asked: "Have you seen the sign up there?" The Italian man said: "Yes, I did." It read "For Gentiles Only", people of another faith than the Jewish faith. So the Italian man said: "I am not Jewish, I am Italian". The person at the door answered back: "That's even worse!" And that is the kind of society we have overcome; that no longer exists today. You do not know how proud I was to tell them: Well, this is your brother the peasouper who is with you tonight. That's what this country is all about.
We have made enormous progress and what irritates me in this debate is that they try to sow hatred in our society. Some people hate us because we are federalists, because we decided to come here to Ottawa and defend the interests of our constituents. It hurts. In recent years, when visiting the province of Quebec, I have seen in meetings young brainwashed Quebeckers who hated me because I am a Quebecker like them, I love my people and 1 come to serve them in Ottawa.
This is what hurts, Mr. Speaker. We probably had some unhappy times in our Canadian history. But today millions of human beings would give their shirt and all their possessions to come and share with us what we call our miseries.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
And it is possible to build a fraternal society in Canada. Arrangements are possible. Everybody wants a new Canadian constitution. No political party wants the status quo. I had some very stirring times Wednesday at the federalist meeting in Quebec. My hon. friend from Joliette (Mr. La Salle) who is here would have been very surprised to see me

April 18, 1980
The Address-Mr. Chretien
sitting side by side with Marcel Masse, both of us speaking for a united Canada. This is what is happening in Quebec. It is possible for people who believe that you can be a Canadian and a Quebecker at the same time. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I have no problem with my identity. It does not give me any problem, I am a Maurician before anything else. I am from the province of Quebec and I am a citizen of Canada. It does not give me any complex. I can be a Quebecker and a Canadian as well.
Mr. Speaker, what concerns me right now is that people are trying to bring about divisions rather than unity. We have received too much from our creator not to open our eyes to our fellow citizens. Canadian society is one of the most democratic in the world. Our country is the freest in the whole universe. You can hold any type of opinion and support any cause you want in Canada, you can have a different language or a different culture, and your government will encourage you to maintain these differences because a person can achieve his potential when he accepts his own personality and adapts it to the personality of others.
When I look at my country, when I look at the progress accomplished in the last 25 years, I see that there has been a lot of change. Seventeen years ago, when I came here, the Canadian Parliament was not the same as it is now. I can wander around the House and see people of all political parties who spend hours trying to learn the language of the other group. This was not the case 17 years ago. There are schools throughout Canada which are full and refused, where Anglophones want to take immersion classes in French. Of course, we do not expect all the Anglophones to become bilingual. People in Shawinigan or Joliette who work in plants can very well go on speaking French only and those who do the same work in Hamilton or Windsor can very well go on speaking their own language. However, the fact that we have two official languages in Canada is not a problem, but an asset, Mr. Speaker. The fact that we have access to the two greatest cultures of the western world is what makes Canada great.
My last function as finance minister was to sign an agreement with the government of Algeria, and I asked the ambassador why he was signing an agreement in which we granted a credit margin of $2 billion to purchase Canadian goods. His reply was very simple. He told me: Because Canada is the only country which can give us North American technology in French. This is Canada. This is why we are accepted as a nation throughout the world. This is why when you sport a maple leaf or hold a Canadian passport abroad, you are always received as a friend, because we are sufficiently developed to help others and have no extraterritorial ambitions.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, we Quebeckers must now think seriously about what the Parti Quebecois is asking, about the true nature of the mandate it has requested.
And I would like to briefly sum up this mandate. It is a mandate for putting an end to the Parliament of Canada; it is a mandate which will make you, Madam Speaker, the first and the last lady from the province of Quebec to preside over the House of Commons; which will make my colleague, Mr. Pierre Elliott Trudeau, the last French Canadian to ever be Prime Minister of Canada; it is a mandate which will guarantee that Quebec men and women will never sit again as elected repre-sentives in the Canadian Parliament. To all of that, Mr. Speaker, I say no. This mandate would put an end to equalization payments to Quebec, would oppose any reform of Canadian federalism, would create a separate Quebec army, take away from Quebeckers their Canadian passport, would deprive them of the riches of Canada, would put a stop to the sharing of the benefits of the Canadian tax system. It is a mandate to increase the taxburden of the Quebec people or lower their level of government services. To all that, Mr. Speaker, again I say no. Finally, it is a mandate to negotiate an outrageous increase in the price of gasoline and heating oil consumed by Quebeckers.
Mr. Speaker, I say no and I invite all Quebec citizens to say no with me because the Canadian experience is not over yet, because we are able to face up to the challenge and be recognized as full-fledged citizens of Canada while assuming all our responsibilities both as Quebeckers and as Canadians. That is why, Mr. Speaker, we will all meet this new challenge with the knowledge that there can be a better Canada and this is why we will reject the mandate requested by the PQ government by saying, no, thanks, Mr. Levesque.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to extend my congratulations to Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Laval-des-Rapides (Madam Sauve), on her appointment to the chair of this House. I extend my best wishes to her, and to you as Deputy Speaker.
I am very proud to be able to speak today on the motion before the House. I am proud to be here as the representative of the people of Selkirk-Interlake. I thank these fine people for having shown their faith in me twice in the past year. I only hope I will never betray that faith.
Although I was rather active in the last Parliament, having risen on a number of occasions during the question period and in Committees of the Whole, I have never had an opportunity to make my so-called maiden speech. I was scheduled to be my party's next speaker in the budget debate last December, but events deprived me of that opportunity.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
So it is with much pleasure that I do so today.
As is customary on the occasion of maiden speeches, I would like to share with the House a brief view of my riding.
April 18, 1980

Selkirk-Interlake lies in central Manitoba, stretching north from the city limits of Winnipeg 250 miles to Grand Rapids. It is bounded east and west by lakes Winnipeg, Manitoba, and Winnipegosis. It is diverse in its makeup. The southeast is given over to urban centres, the west and central parts to agriculture, and the north is a largely unpopulated spread of muskeg and spruce. Scattered throughout are some 12 Indian reserves.
Selkirk-Interlake played a not inconsiderable role in the development of western Canada. It was into this area that Sieur de La Verendrye first led his fur traders from Montreal. It was into this area that Chief Peguis led a band of Salteaux Indians from north central Ontario. In 1812, Lord Selkirk came with his first group of settlers. A few years later these same settlers returned fleeing the massacre at Seven Oaks.
Subsequent settlers included Icelanders who, in 1875, established a colony on the shores of Lake Winnipeg-a colony with its own republican form of government. A few years later came the first Ukrainian settlers to western Canada, followed by Poles and Germans. Among the German settlers were the ancestors of our present Governor General.
From this brief outline, let us turn to look at the concerns of the people of Selkirk-Interlake today. They share with most Canadians a desire to share in the good life that we know that this country can offer us. They share the same frustrations at not being able to share fully in this good life. They share the hardships, both economic and social, that are the result of decades of unconcerned and misdirected government in our country.
Let me be a bit more specific, Mr. Speaker. In my riding there is a large number of farmers. Some are fortunate enough to have some of the best grain land in the west. Others have land that seems to grow rocks better than any other crop. Some run large cow-calf operations; others are market gardeners. All of these farmers are looking to the immediate future with considerable uncertainty. Increases in interest rates and energy costs, and threatened increases to the Crow rates are adding considerable costs to their operations. Meanwhile the price they receive for their product does not keep pace with their cost increases. Indeed, in some cases their prices have dropped. A way of life that is very important to much of Canada, the very continued existence of the family farm and of farming communities, is seriously threatened, and successive Canadian governments do nothing but exacerbate the problem.
Many hundreds of persons and thousands of their family members rely on the lakes bordering Selkirk-Interlake for their livelihood. These are commercial fishermen. They share the farmers' concern about ever increasing costs for energy, and interest rates. They share with their east-coast counterparts an anger at the last government for removing a subsidy which assisted them to upgrade their equipment. Their immediate future is threatened by a provincial government which would like to dismantle the federally constituted Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, a body which has brought stability to the industry and a better standard of living to the
The Address-Mr. Sargeant
individuals. Their future is further muddied by the construction of an irrigation project in North Dakota.
The Garrison Diversion unit has been making waves for years. An International Joint Commission report has confirmed that serious harmful effects would result in Manitoba from the completion of this project. One effect would be the eventual wiping out of Manitoba's freshwater fish industry. Successive government ministers have mouthed assurances that no harm would be done to the Manitoba environment, yet construction continues.
The least fortunate people of Selkirk-Interlake, and those for whom I am most concerned, are the native peoples. Status and non-status natives represent 25 per cent of the population of my riding. They represent a vastly larger proportion of the unemployed. In all native communities unemployment is scandalously high; in some it is in the 90 per cent range for much of the year.
Natives of Selkirk-Interlake are concerned about unemployment. They are concerned about the lack of adequate educational opportunities. They are concerned about the lack of decent housing. They are disturbed about the lack of understanding among the bureaucrats in a bloated Department of Indian Affairs. They ask to be allowed to run their own lives, a not unreasonable request in Canada of the 1980s something that Canadians have struggled and even fought for, for years. Indians ask to run their own lives. It is too typical of the dearth of understanding and of the arrogance of Canadian governments that they claim to know best how to run the lives of our natives One has only to look at the quality of life on most reserves to see how badly these arrogant bureaucrats have failed.
There are many others in my riding, among them women, small businessmen, workers, who all share similar concerns, concerns about where the Ottawa government is taking us. In the past year we have twice gone through the considerable trouble and expense of an election, but nothing has changed. The problems have worsened, and this throne speech offers nothing concrete to turn the country around. It is merely full of tired old platitudes.
Is it any wonder that people in many parts of this land feel alienated from their federal government? Is it any wonder that westerners feel alienated from a government that sends as its ambassador to the west a man who insults western voters for electing so-called eunuchs. To paraphrase my leader, as he so aptly put it the other day, westerners are not alienated from the federal system, we are simply alienated from the practitioners of that system. The people of Selkirk-Interlake share in this feeling and look to this government for better offerings than those made in this throne speech.
We have heard a great deal in recent weeks about the Liberal party's "innovative" plans to represent western Canada. I believe they call it "twinning", and somehow it is strangely related to railroad tracks. The Liberals seem to think that such a plan will put them into touch with the grassroots

April 18, 1980
The Address-Mr. Sargeant
concerns of westerners, but their record, when it comes to responding to the grassroots concerns of their own constituents, is hardly anything to brag about.
For instance, in my riding of Selkirk-Interlake, the unemployment rate has reached an unconscionable level of 9.1 per cent, the highest rate in all Manitoba. A Liberal twin, say, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen), might come to my riding to hear the concerns of westerners, and be told, "Mr. Minister, please help us; we want very much to work so that we can pay our bills and feed and clothe our families, but there are no jobs". Flow would the minister respond to their request? No doubt he would respond in the same way that he responds to that same request in his own riding of Cape Breton Elighlands-Canso which, I would add, has an unemployment rate of 16 per cent plus, the highest in the maritimes. How does he respond to that request from his own constituents? In silence!
Perhaps the minister might, while visiting my riding, meet a fisherman who would no doubt tell him, politely, of course, that he was having a tough time making ends meet because he needed a new fishing boat and the government's freeze on the 35 per cent subsidy on the purchase of fishing boats means he just cannot afford that new boat. The minister has heard that complaint too. The fishermen of Cape Breton are feeling the effects of this freeze as much if not more than their counterparts in western Canada, and yet what has he done for his constituents? I suggest he has done nothing.
On the other hand the minister might have the chance to meet farmers or small businessmen in Manitoba's Interlake and he might ask what was on their minds. They would be quick to tell him high interest rates and high energy costs are just unbearable. A farmer might also add that freight rates for his livestock are reducing him to a subsistence level of farming.
The minister has heard all these concerns from the farmers and small business people in his own riding. We have seen his response to these questions-raise the ceilings for loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act or the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Big deal! For most farmers and small businessmen in Cape Breton or Selkirk-Interlake, that amounts to virtually nothing.
The point of this brief exercise in comparative economic problems is to show the government that there is no need to twin with western ridings to discover what bugs them. Members opposite need only to look in their own backyards to become conversant with the sources of western discontent. The sources of western discontent are those same problems that face their constituents, and the same problems that hon. members opposite have been unable to cope with for the many years they have sat as the government of this nation.
As I have said, there were many omissions from Monday's throne speech, but perhaps the most disturbing for me, as my party's defence critic, was the absence of any announcement that this government intends to launch a full-scale review of Canada's defence policy. Perhaps I should not have been all that surprised by this omission in light of some of the extraordinary statements that have been made recently by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne).
In response to the question of when will a new defence white paper be undertaken, the Minister of National Defence replied:
I don't want to talk about a white paper, when you consider it means a stack of studies and all kinds of evaluation-
He went on to say in addition that he would not mind so much, but white papers were "complicated and, yes, boring". That is right, Canada will continue to flounder endlessly without direction in its defence initiatives because the current minister feels that a white paper would be complicated and boring.
Make no mistake, Canada is floundering when it comes to an up-to-date defence policy that recognizes the reality of changing world affairs. In 1971 the last white paper on defence policy was drafted and presented to Parliament. Since then the government of the day has changed, seemingly at random, Canada's defence role to suit its short-term political needs. This government is planning to spend as much as $5 billion on defence in this coming fiscal year. We, as members of Parliament, and Canadians from all walks of life, have no way of knowing that we are getting the best value for our defence dollar.
While Canada flounders aimlessly in search of a defence policy, the world teeters closer to the brink of catastrophe. Escalating tensions between the United States and the Soviet Union do not bode well for our future. The government's intention to work toward disarmament is truly admirable, but the sincerity of such a statement is quickly called into question when, in the same breath, the government announces that it will buy 137 of the most sophisticated fighter aircraft in the world. The F-18A is not a weapon of peace.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, world peace through disarmament should be the goal of our foreign policy. Canada should take the lead with strong independent foreign policy designed with the sole intent of bringing peace to our world. It follows quite logically that we should be using our defence policy as an effective tool for achieving this goal. Canada can lead through example by demonstrating to the world that peaceful co-existence is possible and that there is no need to join in the great rush to the apocalypse. I note only in passing that the new Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan), like his colleague, the Minister of National Defence, seems also to think that white papers are too complicated and boring, and has shelved that laudable initiative of his predecessor.
In September of last year the U.S. Secretary of Defence said that excessive defence spending was risky. Events since that time have proved him all too right. As super powers heat up their cold war and try to leap-frog each other in military supremacy through huge and provocative increases in defence spending, the fuse of the global holocaust becomes shorter. As Canadians, and as a nation that has tirelessly devoted its energies to international peacekeeping and world disarma-
April 18, 1980

ment, we need to know that our defence dollars are being productively spent and are not simply heightening world tension. A complete and thorough review of Canada's military role could examine how and where Canadian military dollars are spent. All facets of our defence policy could be reviewed- NATO, NORAD, UN world peacekeeping, and the protection of Canadian sovereignty.
At present our NATO forces are divided into two small groups. One, the land group, is composed of roughly 3,000 people, while the second, the air group, is made up of roughly 2,000 people. There are approximately 5,000 Canadians in Europe as part of our commitment to NATO. That, my friends, represents one tenth of 1 per cent of the total manpower of the alliance. We must ask ourselves if this is a meaningful commitment or whether, for our energies, we can better contribute to our allies in the North Atlantic. There is already concern within the Department of Defence that our airfields are so badly protected now that, in the event of a conventional conflict, our new $4 billion fighters would be destroyed before they could take off and fire a single shot in anger. Surely our role vis-a-vis our European allies should be rethought so that it is rational and effective in maintaining a stable and peaceful Europe.
Let me briefly mention here our participation in NORAD. The NORAD agreement was first drafted when the principal threat to American security was the manned bomber. But by now we all know that such a threat is virtually non-existent. In 1975 then U.S. Secretary of Defence, James Shlesinger, said that the threat of manned bomber attack was unthinkable in this day of ICBM's and nuclear submarines because of the strike-back capacity of the United States. In the time it would take for a manned bomber to reach North American targets from the Soviet Union, the world would have been destroyed three or four times over by nuclear missiles.
Canada should rethink its role in NORAD. No one denies that we must be able to protect the sovereignty of our nation, but we must be realistic when we identify those things that threaten our sovereignty. Unfortunately I fear our defence planners have not been realistic in their thinking.
It is this same lack of realism, the fact that our planners seem to live in an action-adventure book world, that has led our party to be so critical of the new fighter aircraft project. We have now purchased one of the most advanced fighter planes in the world to protect North America from an eventuality that is only likely to occur, as General Simonds said in a committee on national defence ten years ago, "if all the Russians are crazy". I am sure almost everyone in this House will agree they are not. Surely this is wasteful government spending to the highest degree. And to add insult to injury, it seems very possible that we have purchased an aircraft which the government in Washington will shortly put into mothballs. The NORAD agreement is now up for reapproval. This government should, at a minimum, ensure that the decision whether to renew is referred very soon to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence for a full and thorough study.
The Address-Mr. Sargeant
Earlier I made mention of one of the problems that maritime fishermen are facing. Another problem has to do with Canada's extension of its territorial boundaries to 200 miles. This extension has meant that problems of enforcement have arisen. Not enough attention is being paid to the need for Canada to be able to protect the sovereignty of its territorial waters. We do not have the patrol aircraft and the naval vessels to allow us to protect Canadian offshore interests adequately. This proposed defence review could address itself to these problems.
I should like at this time, Mr. Speaker, to respond to some comments directed my way a few days ago by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), the former minister of national defence. In referring to my recent suggestion that the purchase of the fighter be referred to a special committee of the House, he once again showed his complete inability to understand a clearly enunciated position. If he had thoroughly read my release he would have known that I was suggesting a special committee, not the standing committee. He would have known that the terms of reference were such that my colleague, the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett), could have made very valuable contribution to such a review. If the hon. gentlemen were to cut through his myopia, he would discover that the NDP does indeed have policies on defence. These policies are consistent with our over-all philosophy. In our defence policies, as in all others, we put people first. We say that the ultimate goal of our foreign and defence policies must be peace. To achieve peace we must seek disarmament. Does it not strike you as strange, Mr. Speaker, that people who seek peace are ridiculed and very often dismissed as being a bit soft?
One of my colleagues in recent days said to me, "The best way to prepare for war is not to prepare for it". It strikes me as sheer insanity that in the cause of world peace the nations of this world are spending $1.5 billion each and every day on weapons of war. If I may quote George Ignatieff from a recent Maclean's article: "The one sure thing about nuclear weapons is that they do not contribute a defence; they can only be a threat."
If I may repeat myself, I say that the commitment of this government to pursue such a path of peace is suspect. In one paragraph in this throne speech the government speaks of the need "to suffocate the deadly growth in the nuclear arsenals of the world", and of the need for arms control and disarmament. Yet I am reminded that only last fall when my colleague from New Westminster-Coquitlam called for Canada to join with those of our NATO allies that were opposed to the placement of nuclear missiles in Europe, not a word of support was heard from these same Liberals. The appointment of an ambassador for disarmament, while very laudable, will, I fear, be no more than cosmetic until such time as this country spends as much on disarmament as it does on armament.
I do not live in a dream world. No, 1 am firmly rooted on this earth in the late twentieth century when it is our misfortune and to our shame that we must maintain armed Forces. However, I contend that we can do a far better job with our

April 18, 1980
The Address-Mr. Sargeant
forces than we have been doing. We can use our forces in a much more positive way, in a way that will better serve Canada's needs and interests. Once we determine these needs it is then incumbent upon us to provide our forces with the best and most suitable equipment. But, as I pointed out earlier in this speech, this government does not seem interested in defining these needs and interests.
It is to the credit of the former minister of national defence that he has once again taken a trip along the road to Damascus, and now sees the wisdom in having an early review of our defence policy. I say that this review must be done in conjunction with a foreign policy review. Our defence policy must serve our foreign policy, and not run off on a completely different track. I repeat that our foreign policy must, as its first premise, pursue peace through disarmament, and that our defence policy must reflect this.
We are stagnating in our approach to rapidly changing world events. In an age when cutbacks and restraint are the catch words for our budget drafters, why are we not taking a long hard look at where we spend our defence dollars? As the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) said at the outset of this debate, "the SI5.7 million for just one fighter is enough to purchase 60,000 tons of rice". Surely, as legislators, we must be sure that every dollar spent on defence is needed. A great American general once said:
Every gun that is made, every warship launched, every rocket signifies a theft from those who hunger and are not fed, from those who are cold and are not clothed.
American President Dwight Eisenhower said that in the 1950s. The defence problems of which he spoke then are as true today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words are to congratulate the hon. member for Laval-des-Rapides (Madam Sauve) for her nomination as Speaker of the House of Commons, and to commend my colleagues for her election. I would also like to express my gratitude to the constituents of Sainte-Marie who re-elected me as their member of Parliament. This honour I am accepting with deep humility, and I would like to assure them of my total co-operation. I note with pleasure in the throne speech important elements that meet the needs of the Canadian people and more particularly the citizens in my constituency of Sainte-Marie, such as the $35 monthly increase in the guaranteed income for the elderly, the reallocation of resources to job creation for young people, women and the handicapped, a lower price policy for Canadian oil than was proposed by the former government, the establishment of a Petroleum Price Auditing Agency, promoting the establishment and development of Canadian businesses through a government-buying policy, as well as assistance to companies wishing to repatriate assets and the revival of the process of constitutional reform.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw your attention to a point which I take to heart, that is the future of Quebec and Canada. We all know that on May 20, Quebeckers will vote on the referendum question as set and I emphasize "set by the PQ." The same party is asking us for a mandate to negotiate the separation of Quebec from the remainder of Canada, a scheme it has called sovereignty-association. It is a well known fact that the leader of the PQ has often objected to the federalists' mention of the word "independence" in the present
April 18, 1980

debate, and stated in the legislative assembly that his party had always advocated sovereignty-association. Following those statements, I checked the PQ platform from 1975 to 1979 and in chapter 2 we find in black and white a reference to accession to independence and on page 62 of the 1978 platform under the title: "Mandate to all representations of the party" the following in paragraph 6 and I quote: The sixth convention asks that an evaluation of federalism be made to show the necessity of independence to carry out the platform of the party. To my knowledge, Mr. Rene Levesque, an active member of the PQ, attended that convention.
Mr. Speaker, the PQ government is promising the Garden of Eden to the people of Quebec. Promises, promises and more promises! At that rate, 1 think they are about to beat the record set by the Parti Rhinoceros for impossible promises. You can find them in the white paper of the Parti Quebecois. This is all very nice, but 1 would like to remind Quebeckers of all the promises the Parti Quebecois made before 1976 and never kept. Elere is one of the very first the party made. It appears in its 1975 program at page 19, and I quote:
A government led by the Parti Quebecois would commit itself to providing all people, including the elderly, with a guaranteed minimum income based on the following principles:
a) the minimum income of a person cannot be allowed to fall below the
poverty line-
I would like to know why Mr. Levesque is keeping social assistance benefits below the poverty line. For example: a single person on social assistance in Quebec receives only $301 per month, and a single person who receives the old age security pension with the federal supplement will get $361 a month as of July 1, 1980, and that pension is indexed every three months whereas in Quebec it is indexed only once a year. I would like to know why Mr. Levesque did not live up to his commitment and why he so quickly abolished the indexing of welfare benefits and decreased, not to say stole, by some $15 million family allowance benefits, when the federal government decided last year to grant a $200 child tax credit. Mr. Speaker, the leader of the Parti Quebecois also made another commitment which is set out on page 21 on the party's program. It says that a Parti Quebecois government is committed to indexing the minimum wage rate to the increase in the cost of living.
Another promise gone up in smoke. On page 24, chapter 9, of the same program, under the heading "Senior Citizens," one finds that a Parti Quebecois government promises to build housing units with rents based on income which will provide, apart from the usual services, superintendent, elevators, laundry facilities, tuck shop, medical services and a lounge. The Quebec finance minister recently informed us that this project will be abandoned next year. This statement appears on page 33 of the Parti Quebecois budget speech.
The Address-Mr. Malepart
In that same program, the government guarantees free transportation for the elderly in urban areas and transportation at reduced fare for intercity travelling. Everybody in Montreal remembers the increase in fares for older people. Moreover, those who live in homes know full well that every three months the Levesque government deprives them of their indexation; who knows what will happen to the $35 the Canadian government intends to give them?
Another promise made by the PQ government on page 27 concerning the education of young people reads as follows:
To implement universal free education at all levels, to raise the compulsory school age to 18, to set up a coherent system of scholarships and living allowances or possibly a pre-salary system.
Just another unfulfilled promise.
Mr. Speaker, how could we believe all the fine promises in the PQ's white paper and in the statements Mr. Levesque and his team have made, when they were not even able to fulfil those they had made before being brought to power?
The PQ's advertising during the referendum campaign reminds me of those finance companies which prevail upon the public to borrow from them without indicating that they charge twice as much as any other institution. That is why the PQ is exerting a pressure on the feelings of Quebeckers to sell them its project, without having the courage to tell them the truth about how much this sovereignty-association adventure is going to cost them.
Mr. Speaker, in 1973 the Parti Quebecois had presented its so-called year one budget but the electorate, knowing the true cost of sovereignty-association, massively rejected the Parti Quebecois and its option for independence. Let us not forget that a Yes vote in the referendum would achieve nothing but maintain uncertainty, and that Yes vote would put our country in jeopardy, as the Prime Minister of Canada put it in his speech to the Parliament of Canada: since provinces refuse to negotiate the association, the Canadian government has no mandate to negotiate sovereignty and Mr. Levesque will not get the mandate to negotiate association pure and simple. Which means that a Yes vote leads to nothing but uncertainty. Can we afford to pay the price for that uncertainty and take the risk of seeing it last until the second referendum? Moreover, who says that in two or three years the PQ, afraid again to present its option honestly, will not use new tactics to perpetuate this climate of uncertainty?
I would also like the chief of the Parti Quebecois to tell us what would be the consequences of a Yes for the 3,000 employees of CBC, the 8,000 employees of Air Canada, the 1,050 employees of Teleglobe Canada, the 600 employees of the Federal Development Bank, the 900 employees of the National Film Board, the 500 employees of the St. Lawrence Seaway, the 500 employees of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the 14,000 employees of Canadian Na-

April 18, 1980
The Address-Mr. Hees
tional and the thousands of civil servants of the Montreal area who work in various federal departments. I would like Mr. Levesque to answer this question.
I should also like to remind the citizens of the Montreal region of the contribution of the Canadian government in the field of social and community aid in 1977-78. With regard to family allowances, the Montreal area then had over 975,000 children and the Canadian government paid the mothers of those children an amount totalling $303 million. Under the heading of old age security, there were 300,000 senior citizens in the Montreal region to whom the Canadian government paid globally over $783 million. Under the heading the New Horizons Program, which program the Canadian government implemented to allow our senior citizens to take a more active part in the life of their communities, the Canadian government paid $1.4 million. Under unemployment insurance, it paid $723 million in 1977.
Under housing, from 1975 to 1978, through Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Canadian government granted loans totalling over $173 million for the construction and purchase of houses and income-producing housing complexes in the Montreal region. Direct loans for public housing there totalled over $102 million. Moreover, the corporation lent in the Montreal area more than $21 million for rehabilitating individual and multiple housing units. And CMHC guaranteed in the same area loans totalling more than $1.5 million from 1975 to 1978. All those direct and guaranteed loans contributed to the acquisition and rehabilitation of 92,199 dwellings. What did the Government of Canada do to help the municipalities? Municipalities in the Montreal area benefitted under CMHC programs, particularly those dealing with municipal infrastructure, neighbourhood improvement, public housing and medium density promotion. CMHC paid the municipalities in the area more than $428 million from 1975 to 1978 under those programs. Furthermore, the Department of Finance of Canada contributed in excess of $16.2 million in payments in lieu of taxes to municipalities and school boards in the Montreal area in 1977-78.
I would also like to remind people of the assistance of the government of Canada to businesses. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce guaranteed loans totalling $18.4 million to small businesses in the Montreal area in 1977-78. With respect to business expansion, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce of Canada paid grants of $2.5 million and guaranteed loans totalling $13 million in the area under the program to promote business expansion and efficiency. In 1978 the Federal Development Bank awarded in the Montreal area 731 business loans totalling $50.5 million. In 1978 the Export Development Corporation concluded with Montreal businesses agreements exceeding $150 million.
Those are accomplishments, Mr. Speaker, not promises like those made by the PQ. In concluding, for all the negative reasons I have outlined with respect to the Parti Quebecois and
for all the positive reasons I have set out in respect of the Government of Canada and because I am proud to be Francophone, a Montrealer, a Quebecker and a Canadian, I will be voting No to the PQ question and I am sure the very great majority of Quebeckers will say No to the PQ proposition.

Mr. Speaker, one of the very important things which Canada must do is to become self-sufficient in oil, thereby enabling this country to get out of the hands of foreign oil producers who are now able to charge us anything they like and cut off our supplies whenever it suits them to do so.
To bring this about the government must first of all introduce a very extensive program of research and development to develop cheaper alternative sources of energy, such as energy produced from the sun, grain alcohol, coal, uranium, the tar sands, hydroelectric sources, solid municipal waste, agricultural and forest waste, unutilized industrial by-product heat, and biomass conversion.
The government must also greatly increase the use of natural gas for heating houses, office buildings, factories and apartment buildings. This can be done by subsidizing the cost of the change-over from present oil-heating equipment to gas-heating equipment, and thus greatly encourage people to make this change.
We have abundant supplies of natural gas in this country. Our supplies of this excellent fuel increased by IV2 per cent during the past year and we have more than 7,000 capped gas wells which have had to remain capped because of lack of demand for this valuable heating fuel.
If we can change over from oil heating to gas heating and develop the alternative sources of cheaper energy which I have mentioned, we can use Canadian oil for transportation and plastics only; become self-sufficient in oil; and become independent of the present costly and uncertain supplies of off-shore oil which our present position makes necessary.
As an example of what can be done to introduce a positive program to bring about self-sufficiency in oil, I would like to mention briefly what my own province of Ontario is doing at the present time. In the area of conservation they have set themselves some tough goals. By 1985 they are aiming to reduce the growth in demand in Ontario for all forms of energy to no more than 2 per cent a year while the annual growth in demand for petroleum will be cut to zero per cent per capita.
To my mind, conservation is the most valuable energy resource we have. It is cheap, powerful, abundant, and easily accessible. All it takes is a little common sense, and in some cases, a little help from the government.
April 18, 1980

The province's new five-year $5 million "Heat Save" energy conservation project, for instance, will utilize thermography and home energy audits to aid Ontario home owners in discovering where their homes are losing valuable heat. Thermography is a process for identifying heat loss by measuring infra-red emissions from a building.
In these "heat pictures", which are taken from an aeroplane, home owners can see where heat is escaping from their homes. Armed with this information, home owners can decide for themselves where and how much to insulate their homes.
Over the past three years, the Ontario government has conducted eight pilot projects in thermography, and home energy audits have reached well over 16,000 home owners. In the process, Ontario has become the world leader in the application of aerial thermography.
The government also has a wide range of projects to develop renewable and recoverable energy. As announced in a major policy document last fall entitled "Energy Security for the Eighties: A Policy for Ontario", the government set targets for solar energy to supply 1.8 per cent of the province's total primary energy needs by 1985, and for municipal, forest, industrial and agricultural wastes to contribute another 3.2 per cent.
These goals are part of the government's target to increase Ontario's capacity to produce more of its own primary energy from the present level of 22 per cent to at least 35 percent by the year 1995. Just a few weeks ago the government initiated a program for the development of energy from waste projects in Ontario. In making that announcement, the energy minister pointed out, and I quote:
If properly utilized, energy from waste and biomass conversion could displace the equivalent of 27 million barrels of oil a year, worth about $400 million in 1979 terms. That's enough to heat one million single family dwellings each year.
Over a 15-year period, the government estimates that the production of energy from municipal solid wastes, industrial, agricultural, and forest waste, unutilized industrial byproduct heat, and biomass conversion will require an investment in 1979 dollars of some $3 billion. The government expects a large percentage of the investment will come from the private sector, with the balance coming from the Ontario government, municipalities, the Ontario Energy Corporation and Ontario Hydro.
The ministry of energy has budgeted $2 million in this fiscal year for cost-sharing in feasibility studies and engineering design work. The ministry will provide preliminary assessments of projects as well, and technical advisory services, once a project is under way. Additional assistance will be available under the Canada-Ontario bilateral program.
The government firmly believes that local governments and private industry have a vital role to play in developing energy from waste projects. Such projects will benefit Ontario's
The Address-Mr. Ferguson
economy and will also make it possible for many municipalities and industries to solve their solid waste disposal problems.
In Hamilton, for example, the Solid Waste Recovery Unit, or SWARU plant, is now operated by Tricil Limited. This plant, commissioned in 1972, has a design capacity of 600 tons of prepared refuse a day. It was the first plant of its type in the world. Tricil has a ten-year contract with the regional municipality of Hamilton-Wentworth to process at least 120,000 tons of refuse a year, and plans to expand its operation to include electrical generation from steam in co-operation with the Ontario Energy Corporation.
In the Sudbury region, Inco Limited and the Sudbury Regional Development Corporation have recently announced a joint plan for a similar plant with a capacity of more than 100,000 tons of waste annually.
The government of Ontario feels that these are just two of the existing opportunities for business and government which are waiting to be developed in the area of new energy forms.
Besides energy from waste projects, industry is becoming interested in producing synthetic liquid fuels, in developing solar energy technology and products, and in devising more energy efficient appliances, automobiles and building products-to name just a few. At present, the ministry of energy is reassessing the potential of synthetic liquid fuels, and the minister of energy expects to be presenting a major policy proposal to cabinet in the coming months.
These fuels, which can be produced from natural gas, coal, grain or other agricultural crops and wood, do have a role to play in our future as a means of conserving conventional fuels. Although it is hard to know at this point in time how much of the fuel market they will eventually comprise, very real opportunities exist for the development of the synthetic liquid fuel industry.
This country has the potential to develop a secure supply of energy compared to other industrial countries. Since security of supply is the major consideration of most industries, this availability of energy would give this country a very real industrial advantage in the marketplace. All we need to do as a country is to grab the brass ring.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I have outlined to the House what a province with initiative, knowledge, and sound leadership is doing to move toward self-sufficiency in energy, in the shortest possible time. I sincerely hope that the federal government will show the same kind of leadership, so that this country may become self-sufficient in oil with the least possible delay.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State, Small Businesses):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I want first of all to congratulate Madam Speaker on having been selected as the Speaker of the House. The qualities of discipline and tact, the firmness and sensitivity that she has shown during her past service in
190

April 18, 1980
The Address-Mr. Ferguson
government will serve all of us well during her tenure as Speaker of this Thirty-second Parliament. This is indeed an historic Parliament to be under the direction of the first woman Speaker. 1 also want to commend my colleagues from Rimouski (Mrs. Cote) and Sudbury (Mr. Frith), who moved and seconded the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, on the excellence of their speeches on that occasion. They were beyond reproach.
The background information they have given the Elouse regarding the parts of Canada they represent certainly assists us all to reach a fuller understanding of our country, with its diversities and its common problems. As the newly elected member for the constituency of Lambton-Middlesex 1 shall, in my maiden speech, take the opportunity to speak about this part of our country-its past, its present, and the potential contribution it has to make to our nation, Canada.
1 want to place on the record my appreciation to the electors of the constituency of Lambton-Middlesex for giving me this opportunity to serve them in this Thirty-second Parliament. The riding is a 6,400 square mile area on the southern tip of Lake Huron, bordering part of one of the world's great seaways. It embraces a blend of agriculture and small business that is unique. It is also rich in history.
In the early 1800s, when our relations with our neighbours to the south were not as friendly as they are today, the victorious battle of the Longwoods was fought in the southern part of this constituency. Later, some of the United Empire Loyalists settled here and carved homesteads from this wilderness land. In the next four decades much of the area in both Lambton and Middlesex counties was settled by immigrants primarily from Ireland, Scotland, and England, who made that emotional decision to leave the country of their birth for a country of their choice. They named their settlements after communities in their homelands, and towns like Glencoe, Appin, and Watford grew, reminding them of their roots. The area prospered and the population increased as the pioneers cleared and cultivated the fertile soil, established their businesses in the context of woollen mills, flour mills, cheese factories, and blacksmith shops, and built their schools and their places of worship.
Historians tell us of a man named Lucas who was forced to leave his farm in New York during this period. He set out to find freedom in Canada. As he proceeded through the Enniskillen swamps, the bedding in his wagon shifted and was dragged along the ground. When he arrived at Watford to spend the night, he was refused lodging because of a foulsmelling substance on his clothes and wagon. He was ordered out of town. A short time later the people in the community realized what the source of the pollution was. It was oil, and after a full investigation the oil industry in Canada was born in my community near a town which was later named Oil
Springs. Shortly after, a few miles away, a new community was established named Petrolia.
Today, more than 100 years after that initial discovery, some of these oil wells are still producing in Lambton county and new ones are being brought into production. These are not, of course, on the scale of productivity we find in other areas of Canada today. It is significant, though, that we are rebuilding part of this old oil field and it is being called Discovery Petrolia, due to be opened in July for tourism in the area. In those early days, the area prospered as a result of the oil industry and the agricultural sector. One of those early pioneers had over 200 oil wells on his property. His name was J. H. Fairbank and he served in this House in the Fifth Parliament of Canada.
It is also interesting to note that another member from the Lambton area was represented in Canada's first four parliaments-Alexander McKenzie, a former prime minister of our country.
Of later note, we in our constituency had the honour of having a very lovely and gracious young lady, Sheila Rose, presented with the Order of Canada at the residence of the Governor General. This was for her work in the field of education and promoting the cause of Canada from coast to coast. The award was very well deserved, I may say.
The technology developed by those early pioneers of the oil industry spread abroad during the following generations. Men went to the Middle East, to South America, to Borneo and other parts of the world, taking their experience and equipment with them. Drill bits are still manufactured in the town of Petrolia for shipment to domestic and foreign fields. To this day, Canadian technology developed by those entrepreneurs is being utilized all over the world. This technology has benefited the world, and as Canadians we can be justifiably proud of our pioneers and of our heritage.
For a number of years at the turn of the century many thousands of people moved to the prairie provinces from my region taking with them their resourcefulness and their expertise in agriculture. There, they were joined by immigrants from all over the world who were making this their country of choice.
In my area, in my lifetime, I have witnessed people from other nations joining us, the Slovak people in the 1930s, the Dutch in the 1950s and the Portuguese in the late 1960s, to name but a few. They came to Canada, a land of opportunity, a land of freedom, and they have made our lives richer by their presence here. I admire their courage and remember that our ancestors too, made this their country of choice. They settled among our native people who still reside in the area today in the communities of Kettle Point, Muncey and Caradoc. It is with pride that these native people contribute and involve themselves in sports, community activities, and society in general.
April 18, 1980

Incidentally, I want to commend the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) on his question of privilege in the House this morning which allowed participants from all parties to express themselves on the issue he raised. I think it was a proud occasion in the House when we saw such unanimity among hon. members about certain comments which had been made outside this area.
I am aware of the traditional differences which historically have developed between the east and the west as well as between individual regions, misunderstandings which unfortunately seem to be increasing in intensity rather than decreasing. Perhaps it is due to the nature of modern day communications that we are instantaneously aware of regional advantages and disadvantages. It sometimes seems we have forgotten the hopes and dreams of the Fathers of Confederation as they struggled to unite this vast and diverse land into one great nation.
If we are to fulfil our duties in this House we must not forget that we all have a common bond-the bond of being a Canadian. Whether we were elected to represent a constituency in the east or in the west, we were elected to the Parliament of Canada. This institution is Canada, and if we are to fulfil our duties as elected representatives we must work for a common objective, and part of that objective is a better understanding of our fellow Canadians and the problems that are unique to the respective regions.

speechtext:
I would suggest that the Speech from the Throne encompasses and reflects our heritage and our objectives when it refers to ensuring, and I quote-
-a strong country with first claim on the loyalty of all of its citizens; a country that regards diversity as an asset, not a liability; a country whose people share their wealth first with those who need it most; a country that encourages initiative, welcomes daring and promotes enterprise and a country which opens its eyes, its mind and its heart to the larger community of nations, refusing to regard its own national borders as the outward limits of the universe.
Ours is a great and beautiful country which has been blessed by vast and diverse natural resources as well as by as great and diverse human resources. We must look ahead in a positive manner and plan to develop, nurture and utilize those resources. Our greatest resource, of course, is our people. Let us give our young people the incentive and encouragement to travel throughout our land so that they, unlike many of us, may understand the diversity which is Canada and the cultures which have given us such a unique identity. I feel fortunate that my children have had the opportunity to travel across this land from west to east to see and understand its vastness and grandeur. I am proud, too, that they have learned to communicate with Canadians whose first language is French as well as with Canadians whose first language is English.
Another potential I am enthusiastic about is the potential of our renewable resources, and again, in this area, we are the
The Address-Mr. Ferguson
envy of the world because we can develop such a variety of energy sources. Like those early entrepreneurs from the oil industry we now find many young and energetic individuals utilizing crop and communal refuse in a manner which will allow us to conserve our non-renewable resources. We are enthusiastic about a more efficient concept of heating being developed by two young men in my constituency, a concept which will utilize materials presently considered to be waste. I trust that the Renewable Energy Corporation will be of assistance to such individuals and entrepreneurs. The alternatives are there and must be utilized as quickly as possible.
The over-all philosophy of the Speech from the Throne was one of a positive continuation of the potential of our nation, and certainly I am pleased to see included the proposal to establish the Canadian Agricultural Export Corporation that will enable our producers to sell abroad as Canadians, rather than seeing one province competing against another for the same markets. Such a vehicle will enable us to focus on specific markets and expand our sales abroad, utilizing the potential of a renewable Canadian resource. We are one of the few nations of the world with mechanisms in place to plan our production for specific markets and to sell on long-term contractual arrangements. The spinoff effects of such as positive move will create new jobs and be a boon to small businesses and the agro-industries in this nation.
These spinoff effects will not only give us a better balance of trade and thereby benefit all of society, but will enable farmers in Canada to work together as Canadians as envisioned by the Fathers of Confederation.
